Explain the right to take part in the plan of service and to be told promptly of changes. Review each service plan and change with the client (SVC-03) and document the client's agreement.
Explain the right to a copy of the most recent licensure inspection report on written request (CR-07).
Explain the client's duty to tell the agency about changes in condition or events affecting service needs. Give the office number [PHONE] for reporting changes.

Obtain the client's or responsible party's signature acknowledging receipt on the service agreement (C9) and give them a copy of the notice to keep. File the signed acknowledgment in the client record.
If the client cannot sign, document the reason, who was present, and obtain the signature of the responsible party.

For waiver clients, also provide the program's own rights and appeal information. The Administrator confirms the current required contents with the DAS (CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP) or DBHDD (NOW/COMP) provider manuals at least annually and whenever the program issues revisions, and updates the packet.
Waiver clients' rights in the home are honored under SVC-17, including HCBS settings requirements at 42 CFR 441.301(c).
Supervisors re-review client rights at each supervisory home visit, and ask whether the client feels respected and understands how to complain. Document the response.
Orient every caregiver to client rights at hire and review annually (PER-03). Caregivers report any suspected rights violation to the supervisor the same day.
The Administrator audits a sample of new client records quarterly to confirm the notice was given on time with all items complete, and reports results to Quality Assurance (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approve the notice, ensure it contains all required items, confirm waiver program contents and audit compliance.
Deliver and explain the notice on time, complete all blanks, obtain acknowledgment and file it.
Honor client rights, respect property and residence, and report suspected violations.
Participate in planning, tell the agency about changes in condition or events affecting service needs, and treat staff with respect.

documentation: Current Notice of Client Rights and Responsibilities form
Signed acknowledgment in the service agreement
Record of explanation, language or format used, and any refusals
Waiver program rights and appeal materials provided
Quarterly audit results
Annual caregiver training record on client rights

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All staff; clients, responsible parties and others who raise concerns
policies.purpose: To give clients and others a clear way to complain, to resolve complaints promptly and without retaliation, and to use complaint data to improve care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts complaints orally or in writing from clients and others and resolves them in a timely manner (C28). We give every client and responsible party our specific phone number, [PHONE], for information, questions and complaints, and the same number appears in the service agreement (C28, C9). The notice of rights names the person who handles complaints with a business address and phone. No client or other complainant is discriminated against or retaliated against for complaining. The rule does not set a resolution deadline, so the agency's internal standard is to acknowledge each complaint within 2 business days and to resolve it, or give the complainant a written status report, within 14 days. A complaint that raises a serious question about services triggers an additional supervisory home visit on a companion/sitter case (C23), and the agency applies the same practice to personal care clients. We keep a complaint file showing each complaint and the actions taken to resolve it, retain it for at least five years (C14), and use complaint trends in the quality improvement program (C26).

definitions.definition: Any oral or written expression of dissatisfaction or concern about services, staff, billing, rights or safety, from a client or anyone else.
The person designated by the agency to receive, log, investigate and resolve complaints: [COMPLAINT HANDLER NAME], [ADDRESS], [PHONE].
Any adverse action, threat, reduced service or change in treatment because a person complained or contacted DCH.
A concern that suggests the client's care is unsafe, inappropriate, not delivered as planned, or involves possible abuse, neglect or exploitation.

procedures: Any staff member who receives a complaint, by phone, in person, in writing or through a family member or other person, records it the same day on the Complaint Intake Form (date, time, complainant, client, nature of concern, staff involved) and forwards it to the complaint handler no later than the next business day.
If the complaint alleges abuse, neglect or exploitation, the staff member also follows SAF-01 immediately. If it alleges an incident or injury, SAF-02 also applies.
The complaint handler enters it in the Complaint Log and assigns a tracking number.
Within 2 business days, the complaint handler acknowledges the complaint to the complainant, by phone or in writing, and explains the next steps.

The complaint handler investigates by reviewing the record, interviewing the complainant, the client and the caregiver, and any other witnesses. The caregiver involved does not investigate the complaint.

Where the complaint raises a serious question about services, the supervisor makes an additional supervisory home visit promptly, assesses the client's condition and satisfaction and appropriateness of services in the residence, and documents it.
The Administrator reviews every complaint involving client safety, rights or billing and approves the resolution.
The complaint handler resolves the complaint or, if more time is needed, sends the complainant a written status report within 14 days, with the reason for the delay and the expected date.
Tell the complainant the outcome and any actions taken, orally and in writing, within the limits of confidentiality.

Tell clients and responsible parties, at admission and again in any resolution letter, that they may call the DCH Healthcare Facility Regulation Division Complaint Intake toll free at (800) 878-6442, or file online with HFRD, if the agency does not resolve a licensing concern. The agency never discourages a client from contacting DCH.

Do not retaliate. Never reduce, reschedule or end services, change caregivers, or treat the client differently because of a complaint. The Administrator reviews any change in the schedule or caregiver for a complaining client for retaliation risk and documents the legitimate reason.
Take corrective action for substantiated complaints, such as retraining, discipline, schedule changes or policy revision, and record it in the complaint file.
File every complaint and the actions taken to resolve it in the complaint file (REC-03). Retain the file for at least five years.
The Quality Assurance lead reviews the Complaint Log at least quarterly for trends by caregiver, client, service type and issue, and reports to the Administrator and governing body (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Log, acknowledge, investigate, resolve and report back on every complaint within the standards stated above.
Review serious complaints, approve resolutions, prevent retaliation and ensure corrective action.
Make additional supervisory visits when a complaint raises a serious question about services.
Accept complaints courteously, forward them the same or next business day and never retaliate.
Analyze complaint trends quarterly.

documentation: Complaint Intake Form
Complaint Log with tracking numbers
Acknowledgment and resolution letters or notes of calls
Investigation notes and supervisory visit records
Corrective action records
Complaint file retained at least five years
Quarterly trend reports

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers who access client information, in any format
federal: 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164 (HIPAA Privacy, Security, Breach Notification), applicable if the agency bills Medicaid or other payers electronically
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of client records and information and to define who may see client records, for what purposes, and under what controls.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps client records confidential. Confidentiality of the record is a stated client right (C28). Employees may disclose record information only to: appropriate agency staff; the client; the responsible party; the client's physician or other health care provider; DCH; others authorized in writing by the client; or in response to a subpoena (C12). This policy states who supervises records, who has custody, to whom and for what purposes records are released, and how long they are retained, as the licensure rule requires (C12). Because the agency bills Medicaid or other payers electronically, it also complies with the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules at 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164. The stricter of Georgia licensure rules and HIPAA governs in any conflict.

definitions.definition: All paper and electronic information about a client, including the service agreement, assessment, service plan, daily service documentation, EVV data, incident reports, billing records and correspondence.
Individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by the agency in any form.
A person authorized in writing by the client or appointed by a court to act for the client.
The standard that limits use and disclosure of PHI to what is needed for the purpose.
An impermissible use or disclosure of unsecured PHI that compromises its security or privacy, subject to HIPAA's risk assessment.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) supervises the client record system. [RECORDS CUSTODIAN NAME] is the custodian of records and controls access, storage, copying and release. The Administrator also appoints a HIPAA Privacy Officer ([PRIVACY OFFICER NAME]) and a Security Officer, who may be the same person.

Store paper records in a locked cabinet in the office at [ADDRESS]. Store electronic records only on agency-approved, password-protected, encrypted systems with role-based access. Caregivers keep client information only on the agency's forms or app and never in personal notes or personal messaging.
Limit access to what each person needs for their job (minimum necessary). Maintain a list of staff and their access level and review it quarterly.
At orientation and annually, train all staff on confidentiality, this policy and HIPAA. Each employee signs a confidentiality statement kept in the personnel record (PER-03, PER-05).
Give each client a Notice of Privacy Practices at the first visit or by the service agreement date, explain it, and ask for a signed acknowledgment. If the client refuses, document the attempt.

Release record information only to the recipients listed in the policy: staff who need it, the client, the responsible party, the client's physician or other health care provider, DCH, persons authorized in writing by the client, or under subpoena.

For a release to a person authorized by the client, obtain a signed written authorization that names the recipient, the information, the purpose and an expiration date, and tell the client they may revoke it. File the authorization in the record.
Before releasing records to a responsible party, verify the person's written authorization or court appointment and file a copy.
DCH may access records relevant to licensure during inspections. The custodian logs the date, the DCH representative and the records provided (GOV-07).

Handle subpoenas under REC-04: the custodian sends the subpoena to the Administrator the same day, and no records are released until the Administrator has reviewed it and, where needed, consulted counsel.
Log every disclosure outside routine treatment, payment and operations, and every DCH access, in the client's Disclosure Log (date, recipient, information, purpose, staff member).

Never discuss clients in public places, on social media or with anyone who does not need to know. Do not take photos or video of clients or their homes except as authorized in writing for care purposes.
Retain client records for at least five years from the last date of service (REC-01), then destroy them securely (shredding or certified electronic wiping) and log the destruction.

Report any suspected breach or loss of a device or record to the Privacy Officer the same day. The Privacy Officer investigates, performs the HIPAA risk assessment, and sends breach notifications to affected clients, HHS and others within the timeframes in 45 CFR Part 164.
Discipline staff who violate this policy, up to termination, and consider any reporting required by law.
The Privacy Officer reviews this policy annually and audits access logs at least quarterly, reporting results to Quality Assurance (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Supervise the record system, enforce this policy, and approve record releases beyond routine disclosures.
Control access, storage and release; maintain the Disclosure Log and destruction log.
Oversee HIPAA compliance, handle breaches, train staff and audit access.
Protect client information, disclose only as permitted, and report any suspected breach at once.

documentation: Signed employee confidentiality statements
Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgments
Client authorizations for release
Disclosure Log including DCH access
Access list and quarterly audit results
Breach investigation and notification records
Record destruction log
HIPAA training records

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, supervisors, office staff and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To protect clients' property, residences and money from loss, misuse and exploitation, and to require bonding, written authorization, accounting and reporting.
policies.policy: Clients have the right to have their property and residence treated with respect (C28). Any employee with unlimited access to a client's personal funds for home management must be bonded through [AGENCY NAME] (C2). Bonding documentation is kept in the personnel record, and a universal bond is acceptable (C13). When home management includes bill paying or shopping with client funds, the service agreement must contain the client's or responsible party's written authorization for access to those funds (C9). The agency prohibits employees from borrowing from clients, accepting gifts above a nominal value, becoming beneficiaries or using client credit cards or accounts. Suspected financial exploitation of a disabled adult or elder person is reportable under O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4 (C34). Every caregiver is treated as a reporter, and staff who learn of suspected exploitation must immediately notify the Administrator, who reports or causes the report. Any staff member may also report directly.

definitions.definition: Tasks that keep the client's home functioning, including shopping and paying bills. Where an employee has unlimited access to client funds, bonding is required.
Authority to use or control a client's money, bank or credit accounts without a cap or immediate review, other than carrying out a single documented errand.
An item of small value, such as a card, a homemade treat or a flower, worth no more than $10, that is not cash, a gift card, jewelry or property.
The illegal or improper use of a disabled adult's or elder person's funds, property or resources for another person's benefit.

procedures: No employee may borrow money or property from a client, lend money to a client, sell to or buy from a client, accept cash or gift cards, be named as beneficiary, agent, trustee or joint account holder, or use a client's credit card, debit card, checkbook, PIN or online account for personal purposes.

Caregivers may accept a nominal gift (worth no more than $10 and never cash, a gift card or jewelry), and report it to the supervisor the same day. The supervisor records it. A caregiver who is unsure whether a gift is acceptable declines it politely or asks the supervisor.

A client who wants to give a larger gift or leave property or money to an employee is told that the employee cannot accept it. The supervisor documents the conversation and the Administrator is notified.

Treat the client's residence and property with respect. Handle belongings carefully, use only supplies and equipment the client allows, and ask before moving items. Report any damaged or missing item to the supervisor right away.

Handling client money is an exception and is allowed only when the service agreement contains the written authorization of the client or responsible party for access to funds (bill paying or shopping), signed and dated by the client or responsible party.

Before an employee has unlimited access to a client's funds, the Administrator confirms the employee is bonded through the agency. The employee's personnel record contains the bond documentation, or the agency's universal bond covers the employee (PER-05).

Where an employee handles money for a purchase, the caregiver obtains the cash from the client, makes the purchase, keeps the receipt and gives back any change and the receipt to the client. The caregiver records each transaction in the client's Funds Log (date, amount received, purchase, amount returned, balance) and the client signs or initials it when able.
Do not commingle client funds with staff or agency money. The agency and its employees do not hold client cash overnight except under SVC-15 procedures approved by the Administrator.

The supervisor reviews the Funds Log and receipts at least monthly for any client whose funds are handled, and compares them against the client's statements when possible. The supervisor documents the review and reports discrepancies to the Administrator the same day.

If the Administrator, a supervisor or any caregiver has reasonable cause to believe a client has been financially exploited, notify the Administrator immediately and follow SAF-01. The Administrator (or any staff member acting directly) reports to the designated adult protection agency (DHS Division of Aging Services Adult Protective Services) and to an appropriate law enforcement agency or prosecutor. Staff are immune from liability for good-faith reports.
Do not investigate the suspected exploitation yourself or confront the suspected person. Preserve records, document facts objectively, and take any immediate steps needed to protect the client.
Remove any employee who is suspected of exploitation from the client's schedule pending the outcome. Do not retaliate against the staff member who reported.
Document the event as an incident (SAF-02) and, for waiver clients, as a critical incident under SAF-08.
Train all staff on this policy at orientation and annually, including signs of financial exploitation, and have each employee sign an acknowledgment (PER-03).
The Quality Assurance lead reviews Funds Log audits, gift reports and exploitation reports at least quarterly (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Confirm bonding, approve any handling of client funds, receive and make exploitation reports, and enforce this policy.
Review Funds Logs monthly, record gifts reported, and investigate discrepancies promptly.
Refuse prohibited gifts and transactions, keep receipts and logs, and report suspected exploitation immediately.
Give written authorization before any funds are handled and review the Funds Log.

documentation: Service agreement with written authorization for funds access
Bond or universal bond documentation in the personnel record
Client Funds Log with receipts
Monthly supervisor review notes
Gift report records
Exploitation report and incident records
Signed employee policy acknowledgments

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], and all applicants and clients
federal: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USC 2000d)
Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101 et seq.)
Section 1557 of the ACA (45 CFR Part 92), applicable if the agency receives federal financial assistance such as Medicaid
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 USC 794), same applicability
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who asks for or receives services from [AGENCY NAME] is treated without discrimination, can understand the information the agency gives them, and can complain without fear of retaliation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not refuse, limit, or end services because of race, color, national origin, language, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, disability, or any other basis protected by law. Georgia Rule 111-8-65 gives clients the right to complain without fear of discrimination or retaliation (Rule 111-8-65-.12(2)(f)). The Rule has no language-access provision, so federal law governs. At no cost to the client, the agency provides interpreters or translated vital documents (rights notice, service agreement, complaint procedure) to clients with limited English proficiency, and auxiliary aids to clients with disabilities. Requests for reasonable accommodation go to the Administrator. The only permitted reason to decline an referral is that the agency cannot reasonably deliver the needed services with qualified staff (see CR-06 and SVC-02). That reason must never be a pretext for discrimination. For waiver clients, the agency confirms any program-specific requirements with DAS or DBHDD.

definitions.definition: A person who does not speak English as a primary language and has a limited ability to read, speak, write, or understand English.
Documents the client needs to understand or access services, including the notice of rights and responsibilities, the service agreement, and the complaint procedure.
Services or devices that give people with disabilities effective communication, such as sign language interpreters, large print, Braille, or amplification.
A change to a rule, practice, or service that lets a person with a disability use and benefit from services equally, unless it would fundamentally alter the service or impose an undue burden.

procedures: At first contact, the intake staff member asks every caller or referral source what language the client prefers for speaking and reading, and whether the client needs any communication aid. The answer is recorded in the client file.

If the client has limited English proficiency, intake staff notify the Administrator the same business day. The Administrator arranges a qualified interpreter (a qualified in-person, telephone, or video interpreter) before the assessment and agreement discussion.

Staff do not ask family members, friends, or children to interpret in place of a qualified interpreter. A family member may interpret only if the client makes that request in private, after being told a free interpreter is available. Document the request and the offer.

The Administrator provides the notice of rights and responsibilities, the service agreement, and the complaint procedure in the client's preferred language, either as written translations or through a qualified interpreter reading them aloud. The interpreter's name or ID, and the method used, are documented.

For clients who are deaf, hard of hearing, blind, or have low vision, or who have speech or cognitive impairments, the Administrator provides the needed auxiliary aid at no cost (sign language interpreter, large-print or Braille documents, written or read-aloud materials, or other effective means) and records what was used.
Staff post and give clients a notice that interpreter and communication aids are free and how to ask for them. The notice states that the client may complain to the agency or to DCH.

Staff must not refuse a referral, limit services, change schedules, or end services based on a protected characteristic. If a staff member believes the agency cannot meet a client's needs, the staff member refers the question to the Administrator, who decides and documents the reason in the file (see SVC-02).

A client or applicant may ask for a reasonable accommodation orally or in writing, to any staff member. That staff member records the request and gives it to the Administrator within one business day.

The Administrator reviews each accommodation request with the client, decides within five business days, and documents the request, the decision, and the reason for any denial or alternative offered. If the accommodation cannot be provided, the Administrator offers an alternative that works and tells the client how to complain.

A client or applicant who believes discrimination has occurred may file a complaint through CR-02. Complaints about discrimination go directly to the Administrator, and the agency does not allow anyone involved in the matter to investigate it.

No employee may threaten, discipline, reduce services to, or otherwise retaliate against a client or staff member who complains, requests an accommodation, or assists in a complaint. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination.
At orientation and annually, staff are trained on nondiscrimination, how to access interpreters and aids, and the prohibition on retaliation (see PER-03). Training is documented.
For Medicaid waiver clients (CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP, NOW/COMP), the Administrator checks with DAS or DBHDD for any program-specific language-access or accessibility requirements and follows them.

During the annual quality review (GOV-04), the Administrator reviews the number of interpreter requests, accommodation requests, and discrimination complaints, and any problems in getting services to people who need language help, and makes corrections.

responsibilities.duty: Arrange interpreters, translations, and auxiliary aids; decide accommodation requests; investigate discrimination complaints; keep records; report trends to the governing body.
Ask about language and communication needs at first contact, record the answers, and notify the Administrator when an interpreter or aid is needed.
Watch for communication problems during supervisory visits and tell the Administrator when a client's language or access needs are not being met.
Treat clients respectfully and without discrimination; report any client communication barrier or accommodation request to the supervisor within one business day; never retaliate.

documentation: Language and communication needs recorded in the client file
Interpreter or translation log (date, language, interpreter name or ID, method, document or topic)
Accommodation request and decision forms
Discrimination complaints and resolutions (maintained in complaint file, see REC-03)
Training records on nondiscrimination and language access

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake and scheduling staff, supervisors, billing staff, and all clients and responsible parties
policies.purpose: To make sure every client or responsible party signs a written service agreement that discloses what services will be provided, the charges, and how to reach the agency and DCH, and to protect the client's right to change or cancel services.
policies.policy: All services provided by [AGENCY NAME] are based on a written service agreement with the client or responsible party (Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)(a)). The agreement contains all ten required elements, is completed within the required deadline, and is updated whenever services, frequency, duration, or charges change. The client may cancel at any time and pays only for services rendered. The agency does not offer services it cannot reasonably expect to deliver (.09(2)). The written notice of rights and responsibilities is given to the client when the service agreement is completed (Rule 111-8-65-.12).

definitions.definition: The written contract between [AGENCY NAME] and the client or responsible party that sets out the services, charges, and other required elements under Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)(a).
The date the agency received a specific request for services.
The person legally authorized to act for the client, with written authorization in the file.
A documented reason outside the agency's control that prevents timely completion of the agreement, such as client hospitalization or an unavailable responsible party.

procedures: Before offering a start date, the Administrator or intake staff confirms that qualified staff are available for the requested tasks, hours, and location. If the agency cannot reasonably expect to deliver the services, it does not offer them and refers the client elsewhere (see SVC-12).

The Administrator or designated supervisor prepares the written service agreement on the agency's approved form, which includes all ten required elements: (1) date of initial contact; (2) referral date; (3) services needed as stated by the client; (4) services to be provided, with frequency and duration; (5) charges and billing and payment mechanisms; (6) acknowledgment of receipt of the rights and responsibilities notice; (7) the agency's phone number for information, questions, and complaints ([PHONE]); (8) the DCH phone number for unresolved licensing concerns; (9) authorization for access to client funds and for use of the client's motor vehicle, if applicable; and (10) signatures and dates.

The DCH number printed on the agreement is the number confirmed with the Healthcare Facility Regulation Division. Complaint intake is (800) 878-6442. The Administrator re-confirms the number at least annually and updates the form if it changes.

The Administrator or supervisor reviews the agreement with the client or responsible party in plain language, using an interpreter or auxiliary aids when needed (CR-05). The client receives a signed copy.
The notice of rights and responsibilities is given at the same time and the client acknowledges receipt on the agreement (see CR-01).

The agreement must be completed by the second visit, if the second visit falls on a different day from the first, or within seven calendar days after services start, whichever is earlier (.09(2)(b)). The scheduler flags the deadline in the client record on the day services are first scheduled.

If the agreement cannot be completed by the deadline, the Administrator documents the good cause and the date it will be completed in the client record (.09(2)(b)1). Good cause is not a routine reason for late paperwork.

If the client or responsible party declines to sign, staff note the refusal and the client's explanation on the agreement and in the file. The Administrator reviews whether services can continue and documents the decision.

The agency states hourly rates, billing frequency, payment methods, mileage or transportation charges (if any), and all other charges in the agreement. The agency does not charge fees that are not disclosed in the agreement. The agreement does not include minimum-hour requirements or non-cancellable terms.

For Medicaid waiver clients, the agreement states that services are billed to the program authorized by the plan of care and that the client is not charged contrary to the waiver plan of care. Billing staff do not collect additional fees unless the plan of care allows it (see SVC-10 and SVC-16).

If the client's services, frequency, duration, or charges change, the supervisor records the specific change and the fact that the client or responsible party agreed to it in the record before the change takes effect (.09(2)(b)2). The agency obtains a signature on an amended agreement when the change is to charges or the main terms.

A client may cancel services at any time, orally or in writing. Staff who receive a cancellation notify the Administrator and scheduler the same day. The client pays only for services rendered before the cancellation notice (.09(2)(c)).

If the caregiver has already arrived at the home when the client cancels, the agency may charge only a reasonable amount for travel and staff time, as disclosed in the agreement (.09(2)(c)). The Administrator approves any such charge and it is itemized on the invoice.

Billing staff issue invoices or statements that match the services actually delivered and recorded in the daily service documentation (SVC-11). Billing questions go to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME]. Disputes are handled under CR-02.
The Administrator audits a sample of new agreements monthly for completeness, deadline compliance, and signatures, and reports results as part of GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Approve the agreement form; confirm the DCH number; ensure agreements are complete and timely; approve any cancellation or travel charges; audit agreements.
Prepare and review the agreement with the client; deliver the rights notice; record changes and cancellations; flag deadlines.
Bill only per the agreement and the services documented; handle waiver billing limits; refer disputes to the Administrator.
Flag the seven-day agreement deadline; relay cancellations the same day.

documentation: Signed service agreement with all ten required elements
Signed acknowledgment of the rights and responsibilities notice
Good-cause note when the agreement is late
Documentation of client refusal to sign
Record of each change in service, frequency, duration, or charges and the client's agreement
Cancellation notes and any travel/staff-time charge
Monthly agreement audit results

policies.title: Client Access to Licensure Inspection Reports
policies.applies_to: Administrator, office staff, and all clients and responsible parties
policies.purpose: To make sure clients can obtain the most recent completed DCH licensure inspection report on request, and to define how and when the agency releases it.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives a client, on written request, a copy of the most recent completed licensure inspection report (Rule 111-8-65-.12(2)(j)). The agency is not required to release a report until it has had the opportunity to file its written plan of correction, which is due within ten days after receiving the written report (Rule 111-8-65-.08(4)). The agency may charge reasonable photocopying fees. The agency logs each request and release.

definitions.definition: The written report issued by the DCH Healthcare Facility Regulation Division after an inspection of the agency.
The agency's written plan, submitted to DCH within ten days of receiving the written report, that addresses the cited findings and may also explain or dispute them.

procedures: The notice of rights and responsibilities given to each client at the time of the service agreement states that the client may request the most recent inspection report in writing (CR-01).

Any staff member who receives a request, whether oral or written, tells the client the request must be in writing, offers help writing it, and gives the request to the Administrator the same business day.
The Administrator records the date the request was received on the Inspection Report Request Log.
The Administrator identifies the most recent completed inspection report in the agency's survey file (see GOV-07).

If the plan of correction has been filed with DCH, the Administrator releases the report within [NUMBER, e.g., five] business days of the written request. A copy of the plan of correction may be released with the report if the agency chooses.

If the report is the subject of a plan of correction not yet filed, the Administrator tells the client the date the plan will be filed (within ten days of receiving the report) and that the report will be released on filing. The Administrator releases the report promptly after the plan is filed and does not delay beyond that.

The Administrator tells the client the photocopying charge, if any, before copying. The fee is reasonable, is based on the agency's actual cost of [COPY FEE PER PAGE], and is waived at the Administrator's discretion. The agency does not condition release on payment of anything beyond the copying fee.

The Administrator delivers the report to the client or responsible party by the method the client chooses (in person, mail, or electronic if secure) and records the release date and method on the log.
The report is released without redaction of the findings. Client names or identifiers of other clients contained in a report are removed to protect privacy (CR-03).
If a client asks about the findings, the Administrator offers to explain them and tells the client that DCH can be contacted using the number in the service agreement.
Requests and releases are reviewed quarterly as part of the compliance review (GOV-04) to confirm that requests are being handled on time.

responsibilities.duty: Receive requests, maintain the log and survey file, decide the timing of release relative to the plan of correction, copy and deliver the report.
Accept requests, help clients put them in writing, and pass them to the Administrator the same business day.

documentation: Inspection Report Request Log (request date, release date, method, copy fee)
Written client request
Copy of the report released and the cover note
Plan of correction filing date

policies.title: Scope of Services — What Caregivers May and May Not Do
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, nurses, personal care assistants (PCAs), companions/sitters, and schedulers
policies.purpose: To define which tasks each type of worker may perform for [AGENCY NAME] clients, and to prevent the provision of unlicensed nursing services or any service prohibited by the rules or other law.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assigns tasks only according to the worker's qualifications and the written service plan. Nursing services are limited to Georgia-licensed RNs and LPNs. PCAs may perform personal care tasks and companion or sitter tasks, but may not provide nursing services unless licensed. Companions or sitters perform only companion or sitter tasks unless also qualified as a PCA or nurse. No employee is assigned a task for which training is incomplete and competency has not been determined, and no PCA is assigned to a client with special conditions without training and demonstrated competency for those conditions (Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(c)). The agency does not provide any service prohibited by the rules or other law (Rule 111-8-65-.09(1)).

definitions.definition: Tasks defined in Rule 111-8-65-.03(n), such as help with bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, ambulation and transfer, and feeding. Vital signs may be taken only in conjunction with personal care tasks.
Tasks defined in Rule 111-8-65-.03(c), such as companionship, supervision, meal preparation, light housekeeping, and transport and escort.

Activities such as observing and reporting changes, arranging doctor trips, picking up prescriptions, accompanying clients to appointments, recording intake and output, reminding clients to take medications, and assisting with self-administration. They never include professional services regulated under practice acts (Rule 111-8-65-.03(k)).
Services provided by a Georgia-licensed RN or LPN under a supervisor, as defined in Rule 111-8-65-.03(p).
Client conditions that require specific training and demonstrated competency before a PCA may be assigned, for example dementia, or a condition identified in the service plan.

procedures: The Administrator maintains a written 'may do / may not do' task list for each worker type (nurse, PCA, companion/sitter). The lists are issued to each worker at orientation and posted in the office.

Companion or sitter tasks (companionship, supervision, meal preparation, housekeeping and sanitation, transport and escort within the limits of SAF-06) are assigned to companions/sitters or to PCAs per the service plan.

Personal care tasks (assistance with bathing, grooming, dressing, toileting, ambulation and transfer, feeding, and vital signs in conjunction with personal care) are assigned only to a qualified PCA or nurse per the service plan.
Nursing services are assigned only to a Georgia-licensed RN or LPN whose license the agency has verified (PER-01). Nursing services are provided only if the agency has opted into SVC-14.
Medically related activities are limited to those in the definition. Medication reminders and assistance with self-administration follow SVC-05. Staff never choose, measure, or administer medication.

The following tasks are prohibited for PCAs and companions/sitters: injections; wound care or sterile procedures; administering insulin or any medication; catheter care and tube feeding unless performed by a licensed nurse; and physical, speech, or occupational therapy. Staff who are asked to do these tasks decline politely and report the request to the supervisor the same day.

Before assigning a worker to a task, the scheduler checks the personnel file to confirm training is complete and competency was determined for that specific task (PER-03). If not, the task is assigned to another worker or the visit is not staffed.

Before assigning a PCA to a client with special conditions, the supervisor confirms that the PCA has completed training for those conditions and has demonstrated competency, and records this in the personnel file.

The service plan lists each task the worker will perform (SVC-03). A worker does only the tasks in the plan. If the client asks for a task not in the plan, the worker calls the supervisor before doing it.

If a client asks a worker to do a prohibited task, the worker declines, explains that the agency's rules do not allow it, and reports the request to the supervisor. The supervisor decides whether to refer the client to a licensed provider or change the service plan.

If a worker is found to have done a task outside their qualification, the Administrator removes the worker from the task immediately, assesses client safety, files an incident report (SAF-02), and takes corrective action up to termination.
The Administrator reviews the task lists at least annually and when the rules change (GOV-03). The Administrator reviews daily service notes quarterly to identify tasks outside scope.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain task lists; ensure assignments follow qualifications; enforce scope-of-service limits; handle violations.
Match tasks to worker qualifications in the service plan; verify training and competency; respond to caregiver questions and requests for out-of-scope tasks.
Assign visits only to workers cleared for the tasks in the plan.
Perform only assigned tasks within their qualification; decline prohibited tasks; report requests and changes to the supervisor.
Provide nursing services within their license and the agency's scope (if SVC-14 is offered).

documentation: Written may-do / may-not-do task lists by worker type, with signed receipt by each worker
Service plans listing assigned tasks
Training and competency records by task
Incident reports on out-of-scope tasks
Quarterly scope reviews

policies.title: Client Intake, Eligibility and Assessment
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake staff, supervisors and nurses who screen and assess clients
policies.purpose: To set a consistent process for accepting referrals, confirming that [AGENCY NAME] can reasonably meet a client's needs, identifying medically frail or compromised clients, and verifying payer eligibility before services start.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts a client only when the services requested can reasonably be delivered with qualified staff under the rules (Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)). The agency records the date of initial contact and the referral date on the service agreement and the date and source of referral in the client file (Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)(a) and (4)(a)). At intake the agency screens whether the client is medically frail or medically compromised. If so, an RN completes the initial service plan and a licensed nurse supervises the client's personal care (Rule 111-8-65-.10(2)(b)). Waiver eligibility is determined by the program's entry point, not by the agency, and the agency confirms authorization before the first visit. CCSP in-home service providers must hold a current, valid DCH private home care license (DHS DAS HCBS 5300 Manual § 208).

definitions.definition: The date the agency received a specific request for services.

definitions.term: Medically frail or medically compromised client
definitions.definition: A client who meets the definition in Rule 111-8-65-.03(j) and therefore requires RN-completed initial service planning and licensed nurse supervision.
A person authorized in writing to act for the client under Rule 111-8-65-.03.
The agency that determines eligibility and authorizes services: Area Agencies on Aging and DAS for CCSP/SOURCE, DBHDD for NOW/COMP, and the ICWP program office for ICWP.

procedures: The staff member who takes a referral records the date of initial contact, the referral date, the referral source, and the contact's name and phone on the Intake Form. The dates are carried to the service agreement.
Within one business day, the Administrator or designated supervisor reviews the referral for requested tasks, hours, location, schedule, diagnoses, equipment, and any known special conditions.

The Administrator matches the request to available qualified staff (PCA, companion/sitter, or nurse) and the agency's scope of services (GOV-06, SVC-01). If the agency cannot reasonably expect to deliver the services as requested, it declines and helps the client find another provider (SVC-12).

At intake, the supervisor screens whether the client may be medically frail or medically compromised under the Rule's definition (.03(j)), using the screening questions on the Intake Form. If the screen is positive or unclear, the Administrator involves an RN.

For a medically frail or compromised client, the Administrator assigns an RN to complete the initial service plan and a licensed RN or LPN to supervise personal care. If the agency has no nurse available, it does not accept the client.

Staff identify any responsible party (such as a legal guardian or agent under a power of attorney), obtain a copy of the written authorization, and keep it in the client file. The responsible party's authority is confirmed before the party signs any document.

For clients who qualify for or receive Medicaid waiver services, the intake staff confirm the entry point: CCSP/SOURCE through the Area Agencies on Aging and DAS, NOW/COMP through DBHDD, and ICWP through its program office. The agency does not determine waiver eligibility or tell a client that he or she qualifies.

For waiver clients, staff obtain and file the current authorization or plan of care, confirm the authorized services and units, and confirm EVV set-up before the first visit (SVC-07, SVC-10). If authorization is not in place, the first visit is not scheduled for billing to the waiver.

The agency does not collect fees from waiver clients contrary to the plan of care (SVC-10, SVC-16). The Administrator or billing staff confirm any client participation amounts with the case manager in writing.

The supervisor or RN visits the home, or meets with the client and responsible party, to assess functional limitations, home safety, caregiver needs, and the client's preferences. The information feeds the service plan (SVC-03). The assessment is documented.

The Administrator or supervisor completes the service agreement under CR-06 and gives the rights and responsibilities notice. The plan of service is completed within seven working days after services start (SVC-03).
A separate client file is opened with identifying information, the date and source of referral, the agreement, the plan, and responsible party documentation (REC-01).
If a referral is declined, the Administrator records the reason and date in the intake log and, when possible, gives the client names of other providers or the appropriate waiver entry point.
The Administrator reviews the intake log monthly for referral volumes, declines, and timeliness (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Decide acceptance; ensure staffing fits the client; ensure RN involvement for medically frail clients; keep the intake log.
Screen and assess clients; complete the service plan; document medically frail determination.
Record dates and referral source; collect authorization and eligibility documents; confirm waiver entry point and EVV set-up.
Verify authorizations and units before first visits; avoid collecting fees contrary to the plan of care.

documentation: Intake Form with initial contact date, referral date, and source
Intake log, including declined referrals and reasons
Medically frail / compromised screening result
Responsible party authorization
Waiver authorization or plan of care and EVV set-up confirmation
Home assessment

policies.title: Service Plan and Plan Updates
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, RNs and LPNs, and caregivers who deliver services under the plan
policies.purpose: To make sure each client has a written service plan developed with the client that is completed on time, kept current, and followed by caregivers.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] develops a written plan of service with the client, the responsible party and, when nursing services are provided and the client has a personal physician, the physician (Rule 111-8-65-.11). The service supervisor completes the plan within seven working days after services are first provided in the residence. Nursing plans are reviewed and updated at least every 62 days. Other plans are reviewed at each supervisory visit (at least every 92 days for personal care and every 122 days for companion/sitter-only) and revised whenever the content items change. For medically frail or compromised clients an RN completes the initial plan.

definitions.definition: The written plan that sets out the client's functional limitations, services, times and frequency, duration, goals, and discharge plans, as required by Rule 111-8-65-.11.

The qualified person under Rule 111-8-65-.10(2) who completes and reviews the plan: an RN or LPN, the Administrator, or other assigned qualified staff for companion/sitter-only services, and an RN or LPN for personal care of medically frail clients.
Days the agency's office is open for business, excluding weekends and holidays.

procedures: On the day services are first scheduled, the scheduler records the first service date and calculates the due date for the service plan (seven working days after services first start in the home) in the client record.

The assigned service supervisor, in coordination with the staff who will provide services, meets with the client and the responsible party to develop the plan. When nursing services are provided and the client has a personal physician, the supervisor also contacts the physician and documents the contact.
The plan includes: functional limitations; types of service; expected times and frequency of service in the residence; expected duration; goals and objectives; and discharge plans.
When applicable, the plan also includes diagnoses, medications and treatments, equipment needs, and diet and nutrition.

For a client who is medically frail or compromised, an RN completes the initial plan (SVC-13). For other personal care clients, the supervisor is the RN or LPN, or other qualified person assigned by the Administrator under the Rule. For companion/sitter-only clients, the supervisor may be an RN, LPN, the Administrator, or another assigned staff member who is qualified.
The supervisor lists in the plan each task the caregiver will perform and checks that each task is within the caregiver's qualification (SVC-01).
The client or responsible party reviews the plan, and the plan is signed and dated by the supervisor. The client receives a copy. The plan is explained in language the client understands (CR-05).
The plan is completed and filed within seven working days after the first visit. If it is late, the Administrator documents the reason and sets a date within [NUMBER, e.g., two] working days.

The supervisor gives caregivers a copy of or access to the current plan before the caregiver's next visit and reviews changes with them. Caregivers follow the plan and report problems to the supervisor.
Nursing service plans are reviewed and updated at least every 62 days. The scheduler enters the review due date in the tracking system.

For other plans, the supervisor reviews the plan at each supervisory home visit: at least every 92 days for personal care and every 122 days for companion/sitter-only (SVC-04). The review is documented in the client file or plan.

The supervisor revises the plan whenever any content item changes, including functional limitations, services, times and frequency, duration, goals, or discharge plans, or when a diagnosis, medication, equipment, or diet changes. The client or responsible party is told of the change and agrees before it takes effect (CR-06).
For medically frail or compromised clients, an LPN may make later revisions to the plan, and the RN reviews those revisions in a timely way and documents the review.

If the client is a Medicaid waiver participant, the supervisor confirms that the plan is consistent with the authorized plan of care and tells the case manager of changes that affect authorized services (SVC-10, SVC-17).
The current plan is kept in the client file (REC-01). Superseded plans are retained under the retention schedule.
The Administrator reviews a sample of plans quarterly for timeliness, required content, and updates, and reports results through GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Assign a qualified supervisor; ensure timelines are met; audit plans.
Develop, complete, review, and revise plans with the client; contact the physician for nursing clients; brief caregivers.
Track the 7-working-day, 62-day, 92-day, and 122-day due dates.
Follow the plan; report changes in client condition or needs to the supervisor the same day.

documentation: Signed and dated service plan in the client file
Physician contact record for nursing clients
Plan review notes from each supervisory visit and 62-day nursing review
Plan revision records with client agreement
Late-plan explanations
Quarterly plan audit results

policies.title: Supervision of Caregivers and Supervisory Visits
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors (RN, LPN, or assigned qualified staff), on-call representatives, schedulers, personal care assistants (PCAs), companions/sitters, and nurses
policies.purpose: To make sure every service [AGENCY NAME] delivers is supervised by qualified staff. The policy sets the home-visit schedule for each client and requires annual written evaluation of every caregiver by direct observation. It also provides nurse access for medically frail or compromised clients, and keeps workers who may be contagious with TB or hepatitis away from clients.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supervises all services through qualified supervisors. A supervisory visit is made in the client's residence at least every 92 days for any client receiving personal care tasks, and at least every 122 days for clients receiving companion/sitter tasks only. Each interval is counted from the date of initial service. A visit is made sooner when the client's level of care requires it, or when a complaint raises a serious question about the services. Personal care for medically frail or compromised clients is supervised by a licensed RN or LPN, with an LPN reporting to an RN, and an on-call representative who can reach a nurse supervisor by phone is available whenever such care is delivered. Each staff member is evaluated in writing at least annually by direct observation or demonstration of the tasks they perform. No employee known to be exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis may serve clients until determined not to be contagious.

definitions.definition: A visit by a qualified supervisor to the client's residence to assess the client's condition, progress, problems, satisfaction and the appropriateness of the level of services. It is documented in the client file or service plan.
A client whose service plan includes any personal care tasks performed by a PCA or nurse.
A client whose service plan includes only companion or sitter tasks.
A client who meets the definition in the rule and in policy SVC-13. Personal care for these clients requires RN/LPN supervision and an RN-completed initial service plan.

A provider representative who is reachable while personal care is delivered to medically frail or compromised clients and who can contact a nurse supervisor by phone or other means to consult with staff on the clients' medical needs.

procedures: The Administrator designates in writing each supervisor and the tasks and clients that supervisor oversees. The Administrator confirms that each supervisor is qualified by education, training and experience (see PER-08) and keeps the designation in the personnel record.

At intake, the Administrator or intake staff classifies each client as (a) personal care, (b) companion/sitter-only, or (c) medically frail or compromised, and records the classification in the scheduling system and client file.

Personal care for any client classified as medically frail or compromised is supervised by a licensed RN or LPN. An LPN supervisor reports to an RN. An RN completes the initial service plan for these clients (see SVC-03 and SVC-13).

On the first day of service, the scheduler enters the date of initial service in the residence and the system calculates the next-due date: 92 days for personal care clients and 122 days for companion/sitter-only clients. Each later interval runs from the last completed visit, so the time between visits never exceeds the limit.

The scheduling system alerts the supervisor and Administrator 14 days before each due date (internal standard). The supervisor schedules the visit with the client or responsible party at a convenient time.
The supervisor makes the visit in the client's residence. Visits by phone or at the office do not count.
At every visit the supervisor assesses the client's general condition, progress toward service plan goals, any problems, the client's satisfaction, and whether the level of services is appropriate.
At the 92-day personal care visit, the supervisor also takes and records the client's vital signs. The 122-day companion/sitter visit covers the same elements but does not require vital signs.

The supervisor reviews the service plan against the client's current needs and caregiver reports, and revises the plan when functional limitations, services, frequency, or other plan content has changed (see SVC-03).

The supervisor documents the visit in the client file or service plan on the day of the visit, with the date, the supervisor's name and title, findings for each element, vital signs (where required), and any follow-up actions. Documentation is completed no later than 2 business days after the visit (internal standard).

The supervisor makes a visit sooner than the standard interval when the client's condition or level of care changes, or when a complaint raises a serious question about the services. The Administrator documents the reason for any early visit.

If a visit cannot be completed by its due date, the supervisor notifies the Administrator at once. The Administrator documents the reason, assigns another qualified supervisor, and makes sure the visit is done as soon as possible. Overdue visits are reported to the QA program (see GOV-04).

Each caregiver is evaluated in writing at least annually by a supervisor through direct observation or demonstration of the tasks the caregiver performs. The evaluation is filed in the personnel record (see PER-09 and PER-05).

When PCAs provide personal care to medically frail or compromised clients, the Administrator publishes a weekly on-call schedule naming a provider representative and a nurse supervisor who can be reached by phone. The schedule is posted for caregivers and kept on file.

A supervisor who learns that an employee has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis removes that employee from client contact immediately. The employee does not return until a healthcare professional determines in writing that the employee is not contagious (see PER-04 and SAF-07).
Each month the Administrator reviews supervisory visit timeliness, on-call coverage and annual evaluation completion, and reports the results to the QA committee.

responsibilities.duty: Designates qualified supervisors, makes sure all visits and evaluations are completed on time, arranges on-call coverage, and reviews overdue items monthly.

responsibilities.role: Supervisor (RN, LPN, or assigned qualified staff)
responsibilities.duty: Makes the visits, takes vital signs at personal care visits, documents findings, revises service plans, and evaluates caregivers in writing each year.
Completes initial service plans for medically frail or compromised clients, supervises the LPN, and is reachable by the on-call representative.
Stays reachable during personal care for medically frail or compromised clients and contacts the nurse supervisor to consult with staff.
Enters the initial service date, maintains next-due dates, and sends the 14-day alerts.
Cooperate with supervisory visits and observations, and report changes in the client's condition to the supervisor.

documentation: Supervisory visit note in the client file or service plan (date, supervisor, findings, vital signs where required, follow-up)
Next-due-date tracking report and overdue-visit log
Written annual caregiver evaluation in the personnel record
Supervisor designation and qualification record
Weekly on-call schedule
Records of any employee removed from service for TB or hepatitis exposure and the clearance determination

policies.title: Medication Assistance and Self-Administration Support (Medically Related Activities)
policies.applies_to: All PCAs, companions/sitters, nurses, supervisors, and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To define the limited medication-related help non-nurse caregivers may give, to prevent caregivers from performing professional services outside their scope, and to make sure medication errors are reported and documented.
policies.policy: Georgia's Private Home Care Provider rule has no provision allowing non-nurse caregivers to administer medications. At [AGENCY NAME], PCAs and companions/sitters may only remind clients to take their medications and assist clients who are self-administering. They may also pick up prescriptions and accompany clients to appointments. Caregivers do not select, measure, draw up, inject, or give medication to a client, and they do not perform any activity that is a professional service under state practice and licensing laws. Nurses may administer medications only within their license scope and only as the service plan directs, and only if the agency has adopted the nursing module (SVC-14). A significant medication error is an unusual occurrence that must be documented, kept at least five years, and reported to the supervisor the same day.

definitions.definition: Reminding clients to take their medication and assisting with self-administration, along with other activities in the rule's definition, excluding professional services.
Verbally or visually prompting the client that it is time to take medication the client has chosen to take, without handling the medication on the client's behalf.
Helping a client who is taking his or her own medication, such as bringing the client's own container within reach, while the client makes the decisions and takes the medication themselves.
A medication event that harms or could reasonably harm the client, such as a wrong dose, wrong time, missed dose, or wrong person, including a caregiver action outside the permitted scope.
An event such as a fall, accident or significant medication error that must be documented and retained for at least five years.

procedures: At intake and assessment, the supervisor records the client's current medications, the prescriber's instructions, and who manages them. The supervisor identifies whether the client can self-administer.

The supervisor lists the medications in the service plan where applicable, and writes the caregiver's role in plain terms, for example 'verbal reminder at 8 a.m.'. The plan does not authorize caregivers to give medication.
Before a caregiver works with a client, the supervisor reviews the plan with the caregiver and confirms the caregiver understands the limits of medication help.

Caregivers may remind the client to take medications, and may assist a client who is self-administering as described in the plan. The client makes the decision to take the medication and does the taking.

Caregivers do not select, measure, draw up, inject, crush, mix, or give medications for the client. They do not tell the client to change a dose or stop a medication, and they do not give medical advice.

If a client asks a caregiver to do something outside this scope, the caregiver politely declines, explains the limit, and calls the supervisor. Caregivers may not make an exception, even when the client or family asks or consents.
Caregivers may pick up prescriptions and accompany clients to appointments when listed in the service plan, and must follow the client funds rules in SVC-15 when handling money for prescriptions.

If a client who needs hands-on administration has no one to do it, the supervisor notifies the client or responsible party that the agency cannot provide this service. The supervisor then arranges for a licensed nurse within the agency (if SVC-14 applies) or refers the client to another provider or the prescriber, and documents the outcome.
Caregivers report to the supervisor the same day any refusal of medication, missed dose, apparent side effect, medication found in an unsafe place, or any change in the client's condition.
If a medication error or suspected error occurs, the caregiver first ensures the client's safety. The caregiver calls 911 for any emergency, then calls the supervisor right away.
The supervisor contacts the nurse or client's prescriber for guidance as needed and informs the client's responsible party.
The caregiver completes an incident report the same day, and the supervisor completes a follow-up note describing actions taken (see SAF-02).
The Administrator reviews each medication-related incident within 2 business days, decides on corrective action such as retraining or removal from the assignment, and records the action.
Medication incident reports and unusual occurrence records are kept at least five years in the incident file (see REC-03).
All caregivers are trained on this scope limit during orientation and in annual in-service training, with the training recorded in the personnel record (see PER-03).
QA reviews medication-related incidents and scope questions at least quarterly (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure caregivers are trained on the scope limit, reviews medication incidents, and ensures corrective action.
Records medications and the caregiver's role in the service plan, guides caregivers, and follows up on errors.
Limit themselves to reminding and assisting with self-administration, report problems the same day, and decline out-of-scope requests.
Administer medications only within their license and as directed in the service plan.

documentation: Service plan listing medications and the caregiver's permitted role
Daily visit notes showing reminders given or refusals reported
Incident report and supervisor follow-up for each medication error
Orientation and annual in-service records on medication scope
Referral or decline documentation where a client needs more help than the agency can provide

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Administrator, schedulers, supervisors, PCAs, companions/sitters, and nurses
policies.purpose: To make sure scheduled services are delivered by qualified staff, that missed and late visits are handled quickly, and that clients are never left without care or information if [AGENCY NAME] cannot staff a visit.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps enough qualified staff to deliver the services described in its service agreements and does not accept services it cannot reasonably deliver. Employees follow the service plan. Only workers who are qualified for the assigned tasks and any special conditions are scheduled. If [AGENCY NAME] becomes aware it cannot deliver services because of an unexpected staff shortage, it advises the client the same day and refers the client to another provider if the client wishes. Every visit and the tasks actually performed are documented. Every missed or late visit is logged and reviewed.

definitions.definition: A scheduled visit that does not occur, or that occurs without the agreed services being performed.
A visit that starts after the agreed start time by more than [LATE VISIT THRESHOLD, e.g., 30 minutes] without client agreement.
A sudden loss of available qualified staff, such as call-outs or resignations, that prevents the agency from delivering scheduled services.
Arrangements to ensure the client continues to receive needed services, including replacement staff or referral to another provider.

procedures: Before accepting a referral, the Administrator confirms that the agency has qualified staff available for the requested hours, tasks, and any special conditions. If not, the Administrator declines the referral and, if requested, refers the person elsewhere.
The scheduler assigns only workers whose qualifications and documented competency match the tasks in the service plan, including any client special conditions (see PER-01 and PER-03).

The scheduler gives each caregiver a written or electronic schedule that shows the client, address, times and tasks, and gives the client the name of the assigned caregiver and the office phone number [PHONE].
Caregivers follow the service plan for each visit and record the services actually performed (see SVC-11).
A caregiver who cannot attend a visit calls the office [PHONE] as early as possible, and no later than [MINIMUM NOTICE, e.g., 2 hours] before the visit, and does not simply notify the client.
The scheduler immediately looks for a qualified replacement, using the on-call list and part-time staff, and confirms the replacement understands the service plan.
The scheduler calls the client or responsible party the same day to report the change and give the replacement's name or arrival time.

If no qualified replacement can be found, the scheduler notifies the Administrator, who calls the client the same day, explains the situation, and offers a rescheduled time or a referral to another provider if the client wishes.
If a caregiver does not arrive and is not reachable, the scheduler calls the caregiver, and if there is no answer within 15 minutes, treats it as a missed visit and follows steps 6 through 8.

For clients who cannot be left without care (for example, those who cannot call for help), the supervisor contacts the client or responsible party immediately, and if a safety concern exists, requests a welfare check through 911 (see SVC-08).

If a caregiver arrives and the client is not home or does not answer, the caregiver calls the office. The supervisor attempts to reach the client and emergency contact before the caregiver leaves, and the outcome is documented.
The scheduler records every missed or late visit in the missed-visit log with date, client, caregiver, reason, time of notice, action taken, and whether a replacement or referral was provided.
For waiver clients, the supervisor reports missed visits to the payer or case manager as the program requires and confirms the deadline in the current program manual (see SVC-10).
For every referral to another provider, the Administrator records the date, provider contacted, and the client's decision in the client file.
The Administrator reviews the missed-visit log weekly and reports the number and causes of missed visits, and any recurring staffing gaps, to the QA committee monthly (see GOV-04 and SVC-12).
The Administrator uses the review to adjust hiring, on-call coverage, and intake limits so that the agency does not take on more hours than it can staff.

responsibilities.duty: Keeps enough qualified staff for all service agreements, contacts clients when there is an unexpected shortage, and approves intake limits.
Matches workers to tasks, finds replacements, notifies clients, and maintains the missed-visit log.
Covers urgent client-safety concerns, reports missed visits for waiver clients, and reviews trends.
Follow the service plan, give early notice of absences, and document services actually performed.

documentation: Schedules and assignment records
Missed and late visit log
Client notification and referral notes
Daily visit documentation
Waiver payer or case manager notifications
QA reports on missed visits and staffing

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Timekeeping
policies.applies_to: Administrator, billing staff, schedulers, supervisors, PCAs, companions/sitters, and nurses delivering Medicaid-funded personal care
policies.purpose: To make sure every Medicaid-funded personal care visit is electronically verified in Georgia's EVV system and that time and task records for all clients, including private-pay clients, are accurate. These records support billing and payroll.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses Georgia's state EVV system, Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+ (MCG+), for Medicaid-financed personal care services. Each verified visit captures the type of service, the recipient, the provider, the date of service, the location, and the start and end times. Claims are submitted through GAMMIS and must match the verified visits. Waiver personal support is billed under T1019 with TF/UC modifiers for CCSP/SOURCE (waiver IDs 590/930) and T2025 for ICWP (660) and NOW/COMP (680/681). Private-pay visits are recorded in an internal time and task record because the rule requires daily documentation of services actually performed. Manual edits to EVV data require a reason code, supervisor approval and an audit trail. The Administrator verifies with DCH which of the agency's billing codes and claim types are subject to EVV and from what date. DCH's EVV page states that claims for Home Health/HHCS with dates of service on or after September 14, 2026 must be submitted through EVV.

definitions.definition: Electronic Visit Verification, a system that electronically captures the required data elements of each visit at the time of service.
Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+, Georgia's state-designated EVV system.
The Georgia Medicaid Management Information System, used for claims submission.
A change to EVV visit data made by someone other than the caregiver at the time of the visit, such as correcting a missed clock-in.
The internal record of the hours worked and the tasks performed at each visit, used for private-pay clients and as a backup for payroll.

procedures: The Administrator designates an EVV coordinator and a backup, and records the designation in the policy file.

The EVV coordinator confirms with DCH Medicaid (EVV Customer Support at (833) 483-5587) which of the agency's programs and codes require EVV and from what date, and records the answer with the date and name of the contact. The coordinator re-checks this at least every six months and when DCH issues a notice.
The EVV coordinator sets up each Medicaid client and caregiver in MCG+ before the first visit, using the authorization details from the payer or case manager.
During orientation, each caregiver is trained on MCG+ and demonstrates clocking in and out. The training is recorded in the personnel record.

At every Medicaid visit, the caregiver clocks in on arrival and clocks out on departure using the approved device, at the client's residence, so that service type, recipient, provider, date, location and start/end times are captured. Caregivers do not clock in or out for another worker, and do not clock in before arriving.

If the system fails, the caregiver calls the office at once, records the actual times and tasks on the paper backup form, and has the client or responsible party sign when able. The coordinator enters a manual edit with the reason code the same or next business day.
All manual edits require a reason code, the supervisor's approval and an audit trail showing who changed what and when. Edits are never used to adjust times to match an authorization.
The EVV coordinator reviews all manual edits weekly, looks for patterns by worker or client, and reports patterns to the Administrator.
Weekly, the coordinator reconciles EVV visits against schedules and daily documentation, and resolves exceptions such as missed clock-ins, location mismatches and visits with no matching schedule.

Billing staff submit claims through GAMMIS only for verified visits and services actually delivered, using the correct code and modifiers (see SVC-16). Visits that cannot be verified are held for review by the Administrator.
For private-pay clients, caregivers record the start and end time and the tasks performed on each visit in the agency's time and task record (see SVC-11).
Payroll uses the verified and approved time records to pay caregivers for all hours worked, including travel time where required (see PER-06).
Time and visit records are retained with the client record for at least five years from the last service (see REC-01) and made available to auditors and DCH on request.
Staff who knowingly falsify visit data are subject to discipline up to termination, and the Administrator reports suspected billing fraud under GOV-05.
The coordinator reports EVV exception rates, manual edit counts and claim denials related to EVV to the QA committee quarterly (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Designates the EVV coordinator, verifies EVV requirements with DCH, approves exceptions, and acts on falsification.
Sets up clients and caregivers in MCG+, reviews edits and exceptions, and reconciles visits weekly.
Submit claims through GAMMIS only for verified services, with correct codes.
Approves manual edits and follows up with caregivers on repeated exceptions.
Clock in and out accurately at the client's residence, report system failures, and complete time and task records.

documentation: DCH confirmation of EVV applicability
MCG+ visit records and audit trail
Manual edit reason codes and supervisor approvals
Weekly reconciliation reports
Paper backup forms for system outages
Private-pay time and task records
EVV training records
QA EVV reports

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, supervisors, on-call representatives, nurses, and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure caregivers recognize and report changes in a client's condition, respond properly to emergencies in the home, and get timely consultation and service plan updates.
policies.policy: PCAs, companions and sitters report client needs, changes in condition and any observed problems to their supervisor. In a life-threatening emergency, the caregiver calls 911 first, then notifies the supervisor, then the family or responsible party and physician as authorized. For medically frail or compromised clients, an on-call representative who can reach a nurse supervisor is available whenever staff provide personal care.
