Clients and their responsible parties are asked to tell [AGENCY NAME] about changes in the client's condition. A significant change in condition leads to review and revision of the service plan.

definitions.definition: Any noticeable change in the client's physical, mental, emotional or functional status, or in the home environment, that could affect the client's health, safety or service needs.
A situation that poses an immediate threat to life or health, such as unresponsiveness, chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, stroke signs, serious injury, or a fire.
A provider representative available to caregivers outside office hours who can reach a nurse supervisor by phone or other means.
The person who acts for the client under the service agreement or legal authority.

procedures: During orientation, every caregiver is trained to report client progress and problems to the supervisor and to handle medical emergencies and other incidents affecting delivery of services. First aid, CPR and handling medical emergencies are covered for PCAs and companions/sitters in their qualification training (see PER-03).
At each visit, the caregiver observes the client's general condition and the home, and compares it to the service plan.

The caregiver reports any change in condition, new need or observed problem to the supervisor the same day, or immediately if urgent, by calling the office or on-call number [PHONE]. Examples include new confusion, a fall, skin changes, decreased eating or drinking, new pain, a refusal of care, and unsafe home conditions.
In a life-threatening emergency, the caregiver calls 911 first, stays with the client, and gives first aid or CPR within their training and certification.
After calling 911, the caregiver notifies the supervisor or on-call representative immediately and then, as authorized in the client record, the family or responsible party and the physician.

The caregiver does not delay calling 911 to reach a supervisor, does not move an injured client unless there is immediate danger, and does not give medication or other treatment outside the caregiver's scope (see SVC-05).
If a client refuses emergency help, the caregiver calls the supervisor while remaining with the client and follows the supervisor's direction. The caregiver documents the refusal.

When personal care is being provided to a medically frail or compromised client, the on-call representative answers calls promptly and contacts the nurse supervisor to consult on the client's medical needs, then relays the nurse's instructions to the caregiver.
The supervisor reviews the report, decides whether a nurse consultation, a visit to the home, a call to the physician, or a change in services is needed, and documents the decision and action taken.

For a non-emergency change in condition, the supervisor makes contact with the client or responsible party within one business day (internal standard) and visits the home if the change is significant.
A significant change in condition leads to review of the service plan and revision of its content as needed (see SVC-03). The supervisor completes the review at the next visit or sooner.

The caregiver completes the daily visit documentation and an incident report for any emergency, fall, injury or unusual occurrence the same day (see SAF-02). Waiver clients' critical incidents are also reported under SAF-08.

The service agreement and the notice of rights tell clients and responsible parties to report changes in condition to [AGENCY NAME]. Supervisors remind clients of this at the supervisory visit (see SVC-04).
The Administrator reviews emergencies and unreported changes in condition, provides retraining where needed, and reports trends to the QA committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Observe and report changes in condition and problems, call 911 in emergencies, and document the event.
Responds to reports, decides on follow-up, updates the service plan, and notifies the family and physician as authorized.
Is reachable after hours, links caregivers to a nurse supervisor for medically frail or compromised clients, and logs calls.
Gives medical-needs consultation to staff through the on-call representative.
Ensures training, on-call coverage, and review of events.

documentation: Caregiver reports of change in condition
Supervisor follow-up notes
Incident reports for emergencies
On-call call log
Service plan revisions
Orientation and emergency response training records

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, schedulers, billing staff, and caregivers
policies.purpose: To protect clients' right to cancel services at any time, to ensure safe and orderly transitions when services end or move to another provider, and to keep clear records of every discharge.
policies.policy: A client may cancel the service agreement at any time and pays only for services rendered before [AGENCY NAME] is notified. Each service plan includes discharge plans. If [AGENCY NAME] cannot deliver services because of an unexpected staff shortage, it advises the client and refers the client to another provider if the client wishes. Georgia's rule sets no notice period for provider-initiated discharge. [AGENCY NAME] gives at least 14 days' written notice with referral options, except when the safety of the client or staff requires immediate action. Waiver clients' case managers or support coordinators are notified before services are discontinued. Records are kept for five years from the last date of service.

definitions.definition: The end of all services to a client, whether initiated by the client, the provider, or because of a change in need.
Movement of the client's services to another provider or level of care.
A decision by [AGENCY NAME] to end services, for example for non-payment, an unsafe home, or inability to meet the client's needs.
The last date on which a caregiver delivered a service to the client. The five-year retention period runs from this date.

procedures: At the time of the service plan, the supervisor records the discharge plan for the client, including the conditions under which services will end and likely next steps (see SVC-03).

When a client or responsible party asks to cancel or stop services, in any form, the staff member who receives the request records it the same day and notifies the supervisor. Staff never discourage or delay a cancellation request.
The supervisor confirms the client's request, the last date of service the client wants, and any needs for transition, and documents these in the client file.

Billing staff charge only for services provided before [AGENCY NAME] was notified of the cancellation, and may add a reasonable travel and staff-time charge only if the caregiver had already arrived at the home, as stated in the service agreement (see CR-06).

When the client's needs change so that the agency can no longer meet them, or the home becomes unsafe, the supervisor discusses options with the client and responsible party, including increasing services, referring to another provider, or referring to a different level of care.

If the agency is considering a provider-initiated discharge, the supervisor presents the reasons to the Administrator, who decides and documents the decision and the steps already tried to resolve the problem.

For a provider-initiated discharge, the Administrator gives written notice to the client and responsible party at least 14 days before the last day of service, stating the reason, the last date of service, and referral options including at least [NUMBER, e.g., two] other providers or the local Area Agency on Aging.

If the safety of the client or staff requires immediate discontinuation, the Administrator documents the specific safety concern, notifies the client and responsible party by phone and in writing as soon as possible, and makes referral and emergency contacts, including 911 or Adult Protective Services if abuse or neglect is suspected (see SAF-01).

If services must end because of an unexpected staff shortage, the Administrator advises the client the same day and refers the client to another provider if the client wishes. The Administrator documents the call and the referral (see SVC-12).
For waiver clients, the supervisor notifies the case manager or support coordinator before discontinuing services and confirms any notice the program requires (see SVC-10).
The supervisor offers, with the client's permission, to share relevant information with the receiving provider, subject to privacy rules (see CR-03 and REC-04).
On or before the last visit, the caregiver or supervisor collects agency items and returns the client's keys, property and personal documents, and the supervisor records the return (see CR-04).

The supervisor completes a discharge summary within 7 days (internal standard) with the reason for discharge, the services provided, the client's condition and needs at discharge, the notice given, the referrals made, and the last date of service.
The scheduler removes the client from the schedule and EVV, and billing staff stop services and submit final claims only for services delivered (see SVC-07 and SVC-16).
The record is closed and retained for five years from the last date of service (see REC-01). The Administrator reviews discharges for trends in the QA program (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves provider-initiated discharges, issues notices, makes referrals, and reviews discharges for trends.
Documents the client's request or the reason for discharge, coordinates transition, notifies case managers, and completes the discharge summary.
Ends scheduled visits and EVV authorization for discharged clients.
Charge only for services rendered and submit final claims accurately.
Report cancellation requests immediately and help return client property.

documentation: Cancellation request note
Discharge plan in the service plan
Written discharge notice and referral list
Documentation of safety concern if immediate discharge
Case manager or support coordinator notification
Discharge summary with last date of service
Final billing record
Closed record retention date

policies.title: Coordination with Medicaid Programs and Payers
policies.applies_to: Administrator, service supervisor, scheduler, billing staff and all caregivers who serve Medicaid waiver participants
federal: 42 CFR 441.301(b) (plan of care requirements, as applicable)
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] delivers and bills Medicaid waiver services only as authorized, stays in contact with the participant's case manager or support coordinator, and meets payer enrollment, licensure and electronic visit verification requirements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] holds a current, valid DCH private home care license before it provides or bills in-home services under the Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP/SOURCE), ICWP, or NOW/COMP community living supports. We provide only the services, units and schedule authorized in the participant's plan of care. We coordinate with the participant's case manager or support coordinator on changes, hospitalizations, missed services and discharges. We take rates, units, billing rules and payer structure (fee-for-service or care management organization) only from written DCH or program sources. Nothing is assumed from consultants, verbal reports or other agencies. Waiver services are documented and verified in the state EVV system.

definitions.definition: The Elderly and Disabled Waiver programs. DCH handles reimbursement, enrollment and utilization review, and the Department of Human Services, Division of Aging Services (DAS) runs day-to-day CCSP operations, working through the Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs).
The Independent Care Waiver Program, a Georgia Medicaid home and community-based waiver.

Georgia's waivers for community living supports for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. The Department of Behavioral Health and Developmental Disabilities (DBHDD) manages the planning list and waiver slots.
The person employed by the program or its designee who authorizes services and maintains the participant's plan of care.
The written, person-centered plan that lists the participant's authorized waiver services, units and frequency.
Electronic Visit Verification. Georgia's system is Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+.

procedures: Before enrolling in any waiver program, the Administrator confirms that [AGENCY NAME] holds a current DCH private home care license (see GOV-02). Only then does the agency apply to become a provider with DCH and the relevant program office (DAS/AAA for CCSP/SOURCE, DBHDD for NOW/COMP).

The Administrator keeps a payer file that holds enrollment confirmations, provider agreements, program manuals and written DCH or program notices. The file is reviewed at least annually and whenever a payer issues a notice.

The Administrator asks DCH in writing whether personal support services for each waiver are paid fee-for-service or through a care management organization (CMO). The written answer is filed in the payer file. Until it is received, billing staff do not assume a payer structure.

Rates, units, authorization rules and billing instructions are entered into the agency's billing system only from written DCH or program sources. Billing staff record the source document and date for each rate.

At referral, the intake coordinator obtains the plan of care or service authorization from the case manager or support coordinator and records the authorized services, units, frequency and effective dates in the client record (see SVC-02).
The service supervisor builds the agency service plan (SVC-03) so that it matches the authorized plan of care. Caregivers are assigned only the tasks and hours that are authorized.

If a participant asks for more hours or tasks than are authorized, staff do not provide them. The service supervisor tells the case manager or support coordinator of the request within 2 business days. The request and the date of notice are documented.

The scheduler checks authorized units against scheduled hours each week. The scheduler alerts the service supervisor when units are near exhaustion or will expire so the case manager can be contacted in time.
Caregivers clock in and out through EVV for every Medicaid personal care visit (see SVC-07). Georgia EVV Customer Support, (833) 483-5587, is called for system problems. Manual edits follow SVC-07.

The service supervisor notifies the case manager or support coordinator of the following by phone or other written method by the next business day: a hospitalization or ER visit, a significant change in condition, a missed or refused service, a staff shortage affecting service, a change in the client's address or caregiver, and any plan to discharge the client. Critical incidents are also reported under SAF-08. Each notification is documented with the date, time, person contacted and response.

When a participant is hospitalized or enters a facility, services are suspended and not billed for that period. The agency asks the case manager for the plan before resuming service and obtains a revised plan of care if the needs have changed.

Billing staff submit claims only for visits that were delivered, verified in EVV and documented in the client file, using the codes required by the program (see SVC-16). Waiver billing codes are T1019 (with TF/UC modifiers) for CCSP/SOURCE and T2025 for ICWP and NOW/COMP.
Billing staff reconcile each claim to the authorization, the EVV record and the daily service documentation before it is submitted. Discrepancies are sent to the Administrator before billing.

The Administrator cooperates with utilization review, audits and record requests from DCH, DAS or DBHDD. Requested records are produced within the deadline stated in the request, and the request and response are logged (see REC-04 and GOV-05).
The Administrator reviews each program's requirements annually, including the CCSP/SOURCE waiver renewal cycle, and updates this policy and the staff training when a requirement changes (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains licensure and payer enrollment, obtains written confirmation of payer structure and rates, and oversees audits and payer communication.
Aligns service plans with authorizations and communicates with case managers and support coordinators.
Obtains authorizations and records them at referral.
Schedules within authorized units and flags expiring authorizations.
Bills only verified, authorized, documented services using written payer instructions.
Provide only authorized tasks, use EVV for each visit and report changes to the supervisor.

documentation: Payer file (enrollment, agreements, written payer structure confirmation, rate sources)
Plan of care and authorization copies in the client record
Case manager or support coordinator contact log
Authorized-versus-scheduled units reconciliation
Claim reconciliation records (authorization, EVV, daily documentation)

policies.title: Documentation of Daily Services Provided
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, nurses, service supervisor and billing staff
policies.purpose: To make sure the services actually performed for each client each day are documented accurately and promptly and placed in the client file.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] documents the services actually performed for each client each day. The documentation is placed in the client file. Personal care and companion/sitter tasks that were actually performed are recorded for every visit. Nursing clinical and progress notes, if the agency provides nursing, are signed and dated by the staff member who provided the care. Caregivers complete their notes at the end of each visit. Tasks are never charted before they are performed, and tasks that were not performed are never documented as performed. Late entries are clearly labeled and dated.

definitions.definition: A written or electronic record of the tasks actually performed at each visit, including the date, arrival and departure times, caregiver and client.
Recording a task as done before it is performed. This is prohibited.
A note written after the end of the visit, labeled "Late Entry" and marked with the date and time it was written and the date and time of the care it describes.

procedures: The Administrator and service supervisor approve a standard daily service note form (paper or electronic) that lists the tasks in the client's service plan, with space for tasks performed, tasks not performed and why, and observations.
Each caregiver is trained on the form and this policy during orientation (see PER-03) and shows competence in completing it before working alone.
At each visit, the caregiver records the date, the actual arrival and departure times, the client's name and the caregiver's name.

The caregiver completes the note at the end of the visit, before leaving the home or before the end of the shift. The caregiver marks each task from the service plan as performed or not performed. If a task was not performed, the caregiver writes the reason (for example, client refused, client not available, unsafe condition).
The caregiver never records a task before doing it. The caregiver never records a task that was not done, and never copies a previous note forward.
The caregiver records observations and changes in the client's condition, and reports any change in condition to the service supervisor right away (see SVC-08).
For Medicaid waiver visits, the times on the note must agree with the EVV clock-in and clock-out record (see SVC-07). The caregiver tells the supervisor of any difference the same day.

A caregiver who forgets or cannot complete a note at the end of the visit writes a late entry as soon as possible. The entry is labeled "Late Entry" with the current date and time and the date of the care, and the caregiver signs it. Original entries are never erased or overwritten. A mistake is corrected with a single line through it, the caregiver's initials and the date.
Nurses document clinical and progress notes for every nursing visit, and each note is signed and dated by the nurse who gave the care (see SVC-14).
Caregivers turn in notes to the office at least [WEEKLY/OTHER SUBMISSION INTERVAL] or upload them through the electronic system by the end of the same day.

The service supervisor reviews notes at least [REVIEW INTERVAL] for completeness, legibility, consistency with the service plan and evidence of changes in condition. The reviewer initials each review.

If a note is missing, incomplete or inconsistent with the plan or the EVV record, the supervisor contacts the caregiver within 1 business day and obtains a correction or a late entry. Repeated problems are handled under PER-07 and PER-09.
Notes are filed in the client's record in date order. They are retained under REC-01.
Billing staff may not bill for any visit unless a completed note and, for waiver clients, an EVV record exist for the visit (see SVC-16).
The Administrator audits a sample of client records each quarter for documentation quality, and the results go to the QA committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Complete accurate notes at the end of each visit, label late entries, and never pre-chart or record tasks not done.
Sign and date all nursing clinical and progress notes.
Reviews notes, follows up on gaps and includes documentation in competency observations.
Confirm documentation exists before billing.
Approves forms, audits records and enforces this policy.

documentation: Daily service notes in each client file
Late entry and correction records
Supervisor note-review log
Quarterly documentation audit reports

policies.title: Staff Shortage Notification and Client Referral
policies.applies_to: Administrator, service supervisor, scheduler, intake coordinator and caregivers
policies.purpose: To keep sufficient qualified staff to serve clients under their service agreements, and to protect clients when an unexpected staff shortage occurs by advising them promptly and referring them elsewhere if they wish.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not accept clients unless it can reasonably deliver the services in the service agreement with qualified staff. If an unexpected staff shortage means we cannot provide the agreed services, we promptly tell the client and, if the client wishes, refer the client to another licensed provider. We keep a current list of alternate licensed providers. The notice and the client's choice are documented in the client record.

definitions.definition: A situation in which the agency cannot staff scheduled services because of caregiver absence, resignation, termination, illness, emergency or another unforeseen reason, and no qualified replacement is available.
Another Georgia-licensed private home care provider that offers the services the client needs.

procedures: Before accepting any referral, the intake coordinator and service supervisor compare the requested services, schedule and location with the staff available who are qualified (see PER-01) and with current commitments. If staffing cannot reasonably meet the request, the referral is declined and the referral source or client is directed to other providers. The decision is logged.

The scheduler keeps a current staffing report that shows caregivers, qualifications, availability and weekly committed hours. The Administrator reviews it at least [MONTHLY/OTHER INTERVAL] and before any growth in clients.

The Administrator keeps an alternate provider list of licensed private home care providers, checked against the state's licensed provider search (GaMap2Care). The list is reviewed at least every six months and records each provider's services and service area.

When a caregiver call-out or other absence occurs, the scheduler first offers the shift to qualified on-call or other caregivers according to SVC-06. The scheduler tells the service supervisor if coverage cannot be found.

If coverage is not available, the service supervisor or Administrator telephones the client (or responsible party) as soon as the shortage is known, and in any case before the scheduled start time whenever possible. The caller explains the shortage, the expected duration and the options.

The caller offers to refer the client to one or more alternate providers if the client wishes. If the client wants a referral, staff give the contact details of at least [NUMBER] providers from the alternate list and, with the client's permission, share the information needed to help the transition.

If the client prefers to wait, the agency documents the client's choice and gives a firm date and time for resuming service. The service supervisor makes sure the client is safe in the meantime and makes the schedule changes needed (see SVC-06).

If a client's safety could be at risk because of the missed service (for example, a client who cannot be left alone or who has no other caregiver), the supervisor first arranges a safe alternative, such as a family member or another caregiver, and follows SVC-08 if there is an emergency.

For Medicaid waiver participants, the service supervisor also notifies the case manager or support coordinator by the next business day (see SVC-10), because the case manager may need to arrange other providers or services.

If the shortage is expected to last or to affect several clients, the Administrator reviews all affected clients and notifies each in writing or by phone. The Administrator stops accepting new clients until staffing is restored.
If the agency can no longer serve a client at all, the discontinuation procedures in SVC-09 are followed, including notice and a transfer plan.
Staff document each shortage in the client record: date and time of notice, who gave the notice, the reason, the client's choice (referral or waiting), referrals given and any case manager contact.
The service supervisor does not bill for services that were not delivered because of a shortage (see SVC-16).
The Administrator reviews shortage events at least quarterly in the QA process (see GOV-04) and takes corrective action on hiring, scheduling or intake limits.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the agency accepts clients only within its staffing capacity, maintains the alternate provider list and approves stop-admissions decisions.
Notifies clients and case managers, arranges safe alternatives and documents the shortage.
Maintains the staffing report and seeks replacement coverage.
Declines referrals the agency cannot staff.

documentation: Staffing report and intake capacity decisions
Alternate provider list with review dates
Shortage notice entries in the client record (date, reason, client choice, referrals)
Case manager notification record for waiver clients
Quarterly shortage review in QA minutes

policies.title: Medically Frail or Medically Compromised Clients and Nurse Consultation
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN and LPN supervisors, service supervisor, on-call representative and caregivers who serve medically frail or compromised clients
policies.purpose: To make sure clients who are medically frail or medically compromised receive personal care under nursing supervision, with a plan developed by an RN, and with a nurse available for consultation whenever staff are in the home.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies clients who are medically frail or medically compromised at intake and whenever their condition changes. A licensed RN or LPN supervises personal care for these clients. An RN completes the initial service plan, and an LPN reports to an RN, who remains responsible for the plan. When staff are providing personal care in these clients' homes, an on-call representative is available who can reach a nurse supervisor by phone or other means to consult with staff on the client's medical needs. Staff assigned to clients with special conditions are trained and shown to be competent for those conditions. The agency does not accept a medically frail or medically compromised client unless nurse supervision is in place.

definitions.term: Medically frail or medically compromised client
definitions.definition: A client whose health status, as determined by appropriate staff under accepted standards of practice, is likely to change or has changed because of disease, injury, disability or advanced age.
A Georgia-licensed registered nurse (RN) or licensed practical nurse (LPN) who supervises personal care for medically frail or compromised clients. An LPN reports to an RN.
A provider representative designated for each shift who can be reached by staff and who can contact a nurse supervisor by phone or other means.

procedures: At intake and assessment (see SVC-02), the intake coordinator screens each referral for conditions or circumstances that may make the client medically frail or compromised, such as unstable chronic disease, recent hospitalization, complex medications, wounds, oxygen or other equipment, swallowing problems, advanced dementia or rapid decline. A positive or uncertain screen is referred to the RN supervisor the same day.

The RN supervisor decides, under accepted standards of practice, whether the client is medically frail or compromised, and records the determination and its basis in the client record. A client who is not determined to be frail is rescreened whenever there is a change in condition (see SVC-08).

If the client is determined to be frail or compromised, the agency accepts the client only if an RN or LPN supervisor is employed or contracted (see GOV-08) and available. Otherwise the agency declines and refers the client under SVC-12.

The RN supervisor completes the initial service plan, including a nursing assessment, before or at the start of services and no later than seven working days after services start (see SVC-03). The plan is developed with the client, the responsible party and, where applicable, the physician, and covers diagnoses, medications and treatments, equipment, diet, functional limitations, services, frequency, goals and discharge plans.

A supervising LPN may revise the plan after the initial plan. The RN reviews each revision in a timely manner, within [NUMBER] business days, and signs the review. The RN remains responsible for the plan.
Personal care for these clients is supervised by a licensed RN or LPN. The nurse supervisor reviews the daily notes and caregiver reports at least [INTERVAL] and records the review.

The nurse supervisor makes a supervisory home visit to the client's residence at least every 92 days from the date of initial service, or sooner as the level of care requires. At each visit the nurse assesses general condition and vital signs, progress, problems, client satisfaction and appropriateness of services. The visit is documented in the client file or plan (see SVC-04).

Service plans for these clients are reviewed at each supervisory visit and revised whenever functional limitations, services, frequency, duration, goals, diagnoses, medications, treatments, equipment or diet change.

The Administrator designates an on-call representative for every shift when caregivers are in the home of a medically frail or compromised client, and posts the name and phone number on the on-call schedule. The on-call representative stays reachable by phone throughout the shift.

The Administrator keeps a current list of nurse supervisors with phone numbers. The on-call representative must be able to reach a nurse supervisor by phone or other means to consult with staff about the client's medical needs. If a nurse cannot be reached promptly in an urgent situation, the caregiver follows SVC-08 and calls 911 when appropriate.

Each caregiver assigned to a frail or compromised client is given the client's plan, the on-call number and the instructions to call the on-call representative for any change in condition, new symptom, fall, equipment problem or question about care.

Before assigning a caregiver to a client with a special condition (for example, a lift, feeding tube, catheter, oxygen, diabetes or dementia), the RN supervisor or service supervisor trains the caregiver on that condition and verifies competence by direct observation. The competency is recorded in the personnel file (see PER-03 and PER-09).

Caregivers do not perform nursing tasks or other tasks outside the scope in SVC-01. If a client needs skilled care, the RN supervisor arranges nursing services (SVC-14) or contacts the physician or case manager.
The nurse supervisor documents each consultation with staff (date, time, caller, question, advice given) in the client record, and the on-call representative logs each on-call call.
The Administrator reviews frail-client caseload, supervisory visit timeliness and consultation logs in the QA process (see GOV-04) at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Determines frail or compromised status, completes the initial service plan, reviews LPN revisions and remains responsible for the plan.
Supervises personal care, reports to the RN and may revise the plan, subject to RN review.
Is reachable during shifts and contacts a nurse supervisor so staff can consult on medical needs.
Ensures supervisory visits, competency checks and plan reviews take place on time.
Follow the plan, call the on-call number for any change or question, and stay within scope.
Ensures nurse supervision and on-call coverage exist before accepting these clients.

documentation: Frailty determination and basis in client record
Initial RN service plan, LPN revisions and RN review signatures
Supervisory visit records (condition, vital signs, progress, problems, satisfaction, appropriateness of services)
On-call schedule and call log
Nurse consultation notes
Special-condition training and competency records

policies.title: Nursing Services (Optional Module — Only If Offered)
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN supervisor, nurses and service supervisor — applies only if [AGENCY NAME] offers nursing services
policies.purpose: To set the conditions under which [AGENCY NAME] may offer nursing services, and how those services are supervised, planned, delivered and documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] offers nursing services only because it employs a fully licensed Georgia RN supervisor. Nursing services are provided by a Georgia-licensed RN or LPN in accordance with nursing practice laws and the service plan, and include regular assessment of the client's needs, participation in developing the service plan, delivery of the services as planned, and reporting of problems and progress to supervisors or the client's physician. Nursing service plans are developed with the client's personal physician if there is one and are reviewed at least every 62 days. Nursing clinical and progress notes are signed and dated. If nursing is not offered, this policy is not adopted and the agency does not advertise or provide nursing.

definitions.definition: Services performed by a licensed RN or LPN under nursing practice laws, as described in the service plan.
The fully licensed Georgia registered nurse employed by the agency to supervise nursing services.
RNs and LPNs holding a current Georgia license.

procedures: Before offering nursing, the Administrator confirms that [AGENCY NAME] has employed a fully licensed Georgia RN supervisor, [RN SUPERVISOR NAME], and has verified the license. Without that RN, nursing is not offered, advertised or accepted (see GOV-02 and GOV-06).

At hire and at every renewal date, the Administrator or designee verifies each nurse's Georgia license (RN or LPN) with the licensing authority's online verification. Staff print or save the verification and place it in the personnel record. Nurses without a current Georgia license do not work (see PER-01).

Nurses must also complete orientation, a written competency evaluation by direct observation or demonstration, TB screening and the other requirements in PER-03, PER-04 and PER-09 before they serve clients.

The intake coordinator refers each request for nursing to the RN supervisor. The RN supervisor completes the nursing assessment, including the client's needs, diagnoses, medications, treatments, equipment and diet, and decides whether the agency can meet the needs safely (see SVC-02).

The RN supervisor develops the service plan with the client, the responsible party and the client's personal physician, if there is one, and contacts the physician to obtain orders or a plan of treatment when needed. The plan states the nursing services, times and frequency, duration, goals and objectives, and discharge plans. The plan is completed within seven working days after services start (see SVC-03).

Nurses perform only the services in the plan and within their license, and follow current physician orders. A nurse who receives a new order or doubts an order contacts the physician and the RN supervisor before acting. Orders are documented in the client record.
The nurse regularly assesses the client's needs at each visit, delivers the planned services and documents them in a clinical or progress note.

The nurse reports problems, changes in condition and progress promptly to the RN supervisor or the client's physician as appropriate, and follows SVC-08 in an emergency. The report and any response are documented.
Every clinical and progress note is signed and dated by the nurse who provided the care. Entries are not changed after signing except by dated, signed addenda (see SVC-11).
The RN supervisor reviews and updates each nursing service plan at least every 62 days, and sooner when the client's condition, orders or services change. The review is signed and dated.
The RN supervisor supervises all nurses and, where applicable, personal care staff. Supervisory visits follow SVC-04.
For waiver clients, nursing is delivered and billed only if it is authorized in the participant's plan of care and permitted under the program (see SVC-10 and SVC-16).
The Administrator and RN supervisor review the nursing program at least annually in QA (see GOV-04), including licensure verification, plan review timeliness and note completion.

If the RN supervisor position becomes vacant, the Administrator stops accepting new nursing clients immediately, arranges a qualified replacement or refers current nursing clients to other providers under SVC-12, and notifies DCH as required (see REC-02).

responsibilities.duty: Confirms the RN supervisor is in place, verifies licenses and decides whether nursing is offered.
Assesses clients, develops and reviews nursing plans, supervises nurses and acts as the contact with physicians.
Deliver nursing services within their license and the plan, document in signed and dated notes and report problems and progress.
Refers nursing requests to the RN supervisor.

documentation: RN supervisor employment and license verification
Nurse license verifications at hire and renewal
Nursing assessment, service plan and 62-day review records
Physician contact records and orders
Signed and dated clinical and progress notes

policies.title: Home Management, Bill Paying and Client Funds
policies.applies_to: Administrator, service supervisor, caregivers who perform home management tasks and billing staff
policies.purpose: To protect clients' money and property when caregivers perform home management tasks such as shopping and bill paying, and to meet the bonding and authorization requirements for access to client funds.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] allows caregivers to shop or pay bills with a client's funds only when the service agreement contains written authorization from the client or responsible party. Any employee authorized to have unlimited access to a client's personal funds is bonded through the agency, and evidence of the bond is kept in the personnel record. [AGENCY NAME] keeps receipts and balance logs for every transaction, requires two signatures above a set amount, and requires any discrepancy to be reported to the Administrator the same day. [SELECT ONE: Caregivers may handle client funds only as described in this policy. / Caregivers do not handle client cash; the service agreement and this policy state this.]

definitions.definition: Activities normally performed by a homemaker for essential home services, such as meal planning, shopping and bill paying.
Authority to access, withdraw or spend a client's personal funds without a transaction-by-transaction limit, for example, signing authority on the client's account or an ongoing debit card.
A fidelity bond purchased by the agency covering employees with unlimited access to client funds. A universal bond covering all such employees is acceptable.
The person with legal authority to act for the client, or the person the client designates in writing.

procedures: The service supervisor decides at intake (see SVC-02) whether the client needs home management services involving client money. If so, the service plan lists the specific tasks (such as grocery shopping or paying named bills), who will perform them and how often (see SVC-03).
For waiver clients, home management tasks are provided only if they are authorized in the participant's plan of care (see SVC-10).

The service agreement includes the client's or responsible party's written authorization for the agency's staff to access the client's personal funds or to shop or pay bills with client funds. The authorization identifies the purpose, any dollar limits and the method (cash, check, debit or credit card). The client or responsible party signs it as part of the service agreement (see CR-06).

If the agency's caregivers will not handle client cash, the service agreement says so and the caregiver may only shop with funds or cards the client or responsible party provides for a specific trip, according to the procedures here, or the client or family handles the money.

Before any employee is given unlimited access to client funds, the Administrator confirms that the agency's bond or universal bond covers that employee. The employee's personnel record includes the bonding documentation (see PER-05). Employees who are not covered are not given unlimited access.

For each shopping trip or bill payment, the caregiver receives the funds or card from the client or responsible party, counts any cash in front of the client where possible, and records the amount on the Client Funds Log. The client or responsible party initials the entry.

The caregiver keeps all receipts and returns the receipts and any change to the client immediately after the transaction. The caregiver records the amount spent, the amount returned and the running balance on the Client Funds Log. The client or responsible party initials the entry.

For any transaction above [DUAL-SIGNATURE LIMIT], the caregiver and the client or responsible party both sign the log. If the client cannot sign, a second agency staff member or the responsible party signs, per the service agreement.

Caregivers never keep client funds in their own accounts or wallets, never mix client money with their own, never use a client's card or account for personal purchases and never borrow money from or lend money to a client (see CR-04 and PER-07).
Caregivers do not add themselves to a client's bank account, take or keep a client's PIN or accept a power of attorney. Caregivers do not buy items for the client other than those authorized.

The caregiver tells the service supervisor the same day of any discrepancy between the funds, receipts and log, any missing money, any suspected misuse of funds by anyone, or any pressure by a client or family member to handle money in a way that violates this policy. The service supervisor informs the Administrator the same day.

If a discrepancy or suspected exploitation is found, the Administrator immediately reviews the records, tells the client or responsible party, and follows SAF-01 for any required reports. The employee is removed from client funds access during the review.
The service supervisor reviews the Client Funds Log against the receipts at least [REVIEW INTERVAL] and at each supervisory visit, and signs the review.
The Administrator reviews the bond and verifies coverage and employee lists at least annually and each time an employee is added or removed.
Completed logs and receipts are placed in the client record (see REC-01) and kept under the records retention policy.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the bond coverage, approves the dual-signature limit and investigates discrepancies.
Specifies home management tasks in the plan, secures the signed authorization and reviews logs and receipts.
Handle funds only as authorized, keep receipts and logs, and report any discrepancy the same day.
File bond evidence in personnel records.

documentation: Signed authorization for access to client funds in the service agreement
Bonding documentation in the personnel record (individual or universal)
Client Funds Log with client or responsible party initials and dual signatures
Receipts
Supervisor review records
Discrepancy reports and follow-up

policies.title: Waiver Billing Codes and Claims Integrity
policies.applies_to: Administrator, billing and scheduling staff, supervisors, and all caregivers who record visits for Medicaid waiver clients (CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP, NOW/COMP)
policies.purpose: To make sure every Medicaid waiver claim [AGENCY NAME] submits is accurate, supported by an EVV record and documented service, billed under the correct code and modifiers, and corrected or refunded promptly when an error is found.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] bills Georgia Medicaid waiver programs only for services that were authorized, actually delivered by a qualified caregiver, and verified through Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) in Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+. Claims are submitted through GAMMIS and must match the EVV record, the caregiver's timesheet or visit documentation, and the authorized plan of care. For CCSP/SOURCE (waiver IDs 590/930), personal support is billed under T1019 with the TF or UC modifier. T1019 is a 15-minute unit and is not used for services identified as home health aide or CNA services. For ICWP (waiver ID 660), services are billed under T2025 with U5 plus TF or TG. For NOW and COMP (waiver IDs 680/681), community living supports are billed under T2025 with U4 or U5. The agency uses only per-unit rates from written DCH, DAS or DBHDD sources and never from consultants or verbal advice. The agency does not bill for services not rendered, for time not worked, or for tasks outside the plan of care. Overpayments are corrected and refunded. No one is retaliated against for raising a billing concern.

definitions.definition: Georgia's Elderly and Disabled Waiver programs (waiver IDs 590/930), approved under Section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act. DCH handles reimbursement, enrollment and utilization review, and DAS runs day-to-day CCSP operations.
The Independent Care Waiver Program (waiver ID 660).

The New Options Waiver and Comprehensive Supports Waiver (waiver IDs 680/681), which provide community living supports for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. DBHDD manages these waivers.
Electronic Visit Verification. It records service type, recipient, provider, date, location and start and end times for each visit. Georgia's system is Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+.
The Georgia Medicaid claims system through which waiver claims are submitted.
Any Medicaid payment the agency received that it was not entitled to, including payment for unverified visits, wrong codes, wrong units or unauthorized services.

procedures: The Administrator confirms before any Medicaid billing begins that the agency holds a current DCH Private Home Care Provider license and is enrolled with Georgia Medicaid for each waiver program it serves.

The Billing Coordinator keeps a current code table for each program: T1019 with TF or UC for CCSP/SOURCE (590/930); T2025 with U5 plus TF or TG for ICWP (660); T2025 with U4 or U5 for NOW/COMP (680/681). The table cites the DCH, DAS or DBHDD document it came from and the date it was checked.

The Billing Coordinator checks the code table against current DCH, DAS and DBHDD provider manuals and notices at least quarterly, and whenever a payer notice is received. The Administrator approves any change in writing.

Per-unit rates are entered only from a written DCH, DAS or DBHDD source. If no written rate is on file for a service, the Billing Coordinator asks the payer or case manager for it in writing before billing.

Scheduling staff open a service only after confirming the written authorization (units, dates, service type) from the case manager or support coordinator. The authorization is filed in the client record and entered in the schedule (see SVC-10).

Caregivers clock in and out through Netsmart Mobile Caregiver+ at the client's home for every visit, as described in SVC-07. Visits with a missing or edited EVV record must be explained in writing by the caregiver and approved by the supervisor.

The Billing Coordinator does not bill T1019 for services identified as home health aide or CNA services. Any question about whether a service fits T1019 goes to the Administrator, who asks DAS or DCH in writing.

Before each claim batch, the Billing Coordinator reconciles three sources for every visit: the EVV record, the caregiver's timesheet or visit documentation (SVC-11), and the authorization. Differences in client, date, time, duration or service are resolved before submission.

Claims are built in 15-minute units for T1019 as authorized and verified. Units are never rounded up beyond the EVV-verified time. Time for travel, training, waiting or tasks outside the plan of care is not billed as client service.

A second person (the Administrator or a designated reviewer) samples at least 10 percent of each claim batch, or all claims if fewer than 20, against source records before submission. The review is initialed and dated.

The Billing Coordinator submits claims through GAMMIS within the payer's filing limit, keeps the submission confirmation, and posts remittances against the claims. Denials and adjustments are worked and logged within 10 business days.

Any employee who finds a possible billing error, duplicate, unverified visit or unauthorized service reports it to the Billing Coordinator or Administrator the same day. If the issue involves the Administrator, the employee reports to the governing body (see GOV-05).

When an overpayment is confirmed, the Administrator stops billing for the affected items, corrects or voids the claim through GAMMIS, and refunds any money received as the payer directs. This is done promptly and within the time the law or payer requires. The Administrator may consult counsel.
The Administrator documents each billing error in a log with the cause, the claims affected, the amount, the corrective action and the date of the refund. Patterns go to the QI program (GOV-04).

The agency screens employees and contractors against the exclusion lists required for Medicaid providers before hire and at least monthly, as part of its program integrity duties under 42 CFR Part 455. It does not bill for services delivered by an excluded person (see GOV-05 and PER-02).
The agency does not knowingly submit false claims or make false statements to obtain payment. Staff are trained on the federal False Claims Act (31 USC 3729) at orientation and annually.

EVV system problems go to Georgia EVV Customer Support at (833) 483-5587. The caregiver notes the problem and time on the visit record, and the supervisor documents the manual correction and the reason.

responsibilities.duty: Owns claims integrity, approves code table changes and corrections, directs refunds, and reports to the governing body.
Maintains the code table, reconciles EVV, timesheets and authorizations, submits claims, works denials, and keeps the billing error log.
Review and approve EVV exceptions, confirm that services delivered match the plan of care, and report suspected errors.
Clock in and out through EVV at every visit, record only time actually worked, and never alter or ask others to alter time records.
Receives billing integrity reports and acts on any concern involving the Administrator.

documentation: Current code and modifier table with source and date checked
Written authorizations and per-unit rate sources
EVV records, exception approvals and timesheets
Claim reconciliation worksheets and second-review sign-offs
GAMMIS submission confirmations, remittances and denial logs
Billing error log and refund records
Exclusion screening records
Training records on claims integrity and the False Claims Act

policies.title: HCBS Settings Requirements and Person-Centered Service Delivery (Waiver Clients)
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, supervisors and administrative staff who serve clients under the 1915(c) waivers (CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP, NOW/COMP)
policies.purpose: To make sure waiver clients receive services that reflect their own choices, preferences and goals, and that their privacy, dignity and control over daily life are respected consistent with their plan of care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] delivers services to waiver participants in a person-centered way. Each participant's choices, privacy, dignity and control over daily activities and visitors are respected, consistent with the plan of care written by the case manager or support coordinator. Georgia's Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP/SOURCE) is approved under Section 1915(c), and the ICWP and NOW/COMP are waiver programs as well. The participant's right to accept or refuse services and to be informed of changes to the plan (.12(2)(b)-(c)) supports this requirement and is stated in the client rights notice. The agency follows the plan of care from the case manager or support coordinator. It does not restrict any participant's rights without a documented, plan-based justification approved through the participant's care team. Caregivers do not impose their own preferences. Program-specific requirements are confirmed in the DAS and DBHDD provider manuals.

definitions.definition: Services shaped by the participant's own goals, preferences, routines and choices, with the participant directing the plan to the greatest extent possible.
The plan developed by the participant's case manager or support coordinator that authorizes and describes waiver services. The agency's service plan (SVC-03) must be consistent with it.
Federal expectations under 42 CFR 441.301(c) that home and community-based services support the participant's choice, privacy, dignity, community access and control over daily activities.
Any limit on a participant's choice, privacy, access to visitors, belongings or daily activities. A restriction is allowed only if the plan of care supports it with documented justification.

procedures: At intake, the intake staff member identifies whether the client is served under CCSP/SOURCE, ICWP or NOW/COMP and obtains the current plan of care from the case manager or support coordinator (see SVC-02 and SVC-10).

The supervisor reviews the plan of care before the first visit and builds the agency's service plan (SVC-03) so that tasks, times and goals match it. The service plan notes the participant's preferences for how, when and by whom care is provided.

The supervisor meets with the participant, and the responsible party if there is one, to ask about daily routines, preferred tasks, food and activity preferences, who may visit, and how the participant wants to be addressed. These are written into the service plan.

When the service agreement is completed, the written notice of client rights and responsibilities is given (.12). The supervisor reviews it with the participant in plain language, including the right to take part in planning, to be told of changes, and to accept or refuse services.

Caregivers are oriented to the participant's preferences before the first visit. They ask the participant how they want a task done and do it that way unless it creates a safety risk. If so, they call the supervisor.
Caregivers respect privacy: they knock before entering, close doors and curtains during personal care, and do not disclose information about the participant to others (see CR-03).
Caregivers respect the participant's control over visitors, phone and mail, daily schedule, meals and use of personal belongings, unless a documented plan-based restriction applies.

When a participant refuses a service, the caregiver respects the refusal, ensures the participant is safe, notes the refusal and any stated reason on the visit record, and tells the supervisor the same day. The supervisor follows up with the participant and informs the case manager or support coordinator as required.

Staff do not apply restraints, seclusion, locked doors, withholding of food or belongings, or other rights restrictions. A restriction is considered only if it appears in the plan of care with a documented justification from the case manager or support coordinator. The supervisor documents it in the service plan and informs the Administrator.

If a caregiver believes a participant's rights are being restricted without a plan basis, including by family or another provider, the caregiver reports it to the supervisor immediately. The supervisor notifies the case manager or support coordinator and the Administrator, and if the situation could be abuse, neglect or exploitation, follows SAF-01.
Participants are told about changes to their plan before or when they happen, and the agency documents who was told, how, and when (.12(2)(b)-(c)).

At each supervisory visit, the supervisor asks the participant if services are done the way they want, if they feel respected, and whether they want changes. The answers are documented and the service plan is revised as needed (SVC-04).

Complaints about choice, privacy or dignity are handled under CR-02. The participant is told they may also contact the case manager or support coordinator and DCH (address and phone are in the client rights notice).
The Administrator confirms the program-specific HCBS requirements in the current DAS and DBHDD provider manuals at least annually and updates this policy and training as needed.
Person-centered practice and HCBS settings requirements are covered at orientation and in annual in-service training (PER-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures services follow the plan of care, reviews any rights restriction, checks DAS and DBHDD manuals annually, and ensures staff training.
Builds the service plan around the participant's preferences, orients caregivers, reviews rights at agreement and at supervisory visits, and coordinates with the case manager or support coordinator.
Follow the plan of care and the participant's preferences, respect privacy and refusals, and report concerns about rights or safety immediately.

responsibilities.role: Case Manager / Support Coordinator (outside the agency)
responsibilities.duty: Develops and updates the plan of care and approves any plan-based restriction.

documentation: Current plan of care from the case manager or support coordinator
Service plan showing participant preferences
Signed notice of client rights and responsibilities
Visit records noting refusals and choices
Documentation of any rights restriction and its plan-based justification
Supervisory visit notes on participant satisfaction
Training records on person-centered practice
Record of annual manual review

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, supervisors, the Administrator and the governing body
policies.purpose: To protect clients from abuse, neglect and exploitation by screening workers, training staff, and requiring prompt reports to Adult Protective Services and law enforcement.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation of any client. Under O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4, a person who has reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult or elder person has been abused (other than by accident), neglected or exploited must report it to the designated adult protection agency (Georgia Adult Protective Services, DHS Division of Aging Services) and to an appropriate law enforcement agency or prosecutor. The agency treats every employee and contractor as a reporter. Staff of a social agency or similar facility must notify the person in charge, who or whose designee reports or causes the report. Staff may also report directly, since any person may report. Reports are never delayed because a supervisor is unavailable. Good-faith reporters are immune from civil and criminal liability (§ 30-5-4(c)). The agency does not retaliate against anyone who reports. At hire, the agency screens out workers with credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation, and obtains each worker's statement at application. The Administrator must also meet the same standard (.09(3)). Abuse reporting is covered at orientation (.09(6)).

definitions.definition: Harm or the infliction of injury, pain, fear or mental anguish on a client, other than by accident, including physical, verbal, emotional or sexual abuse.
Failure to provide the care, supervision, food, medical attention or other services a client needs, whether by a caregiver or by the client's own circumstances.
Misuse of a client's money, property, benefits or resources, or using a client's person or services for another's gain.
A good-faith belief based on what a person sees, hears or is told. Proof is not required before reporting.
The Georgia DHS Division of Aging Services program that receives reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of disabled adults and elders.

procedures: At application, every applicant for employment or contractor status signs a statement that includes whether they have credible evidence against them of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation, and that they have made no false statements about their qualifications (.09(3), .09(5)(a)). The statement is filed in the personnel record.

The Administrator does not hire or retain anyone, including administrators, supervisors or caregivers, where there is credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation. Background and registry checks are completed under PER-02.

At orientation, before working with clients, each employee is trained on this policy, how to recognize signs of abuse, neglect and exploitation, and how to report, as part of the orientation required by .09(6). Training is repeated in annual in-service training.

Any employee who has reasonable cause to believe a client has been abused, neglected or exploited acts immediately. If the client is in danger or needs medical care, the employee calls 911 first and stays with the client if it is safe.

The employee notifies the supervisor or Administrator right away. If neither can be reached, the employee reports directly to APS and law enforcement. The employee does not wait for permission, investigate on their own or confront the suspected person.

The Administrator or designee reports to Georgia APS by phone at 1-866-552-4464, pressing 3 during weekday business hours, or through the online report form. The Administrator also reports to an appropriate law enforcement agency or prosecutor. Both reports are made on the same day the concern is raised, whenever possible. After hours, the report goes to law enforcement the same day and to APS at the next opening.
If the client lives in a long-term care facility, the Administrator uses the reporting process that applies to that setting and documents who was contacted.

A written report follows the initial report. The agency's internal standard is to send the written report within 24 hours of the initial report, or sooner if APS asks. The Administrator verifies the exact statutory deadline in O.C.G.A. § 30-5-4 and updates this policy if it differs.

The Administrator records the date and time of each report, the persons notified, the report or intake number given, and what was said. This record is placed in the incident file (see SAF-02 and REC-03).

The Administrator notifies the client's responsible party and, if the client is a waiver participant, the case manager or support coordinator, unless doing so may put the client at risk or conflicts with instructions from APS or law enforcement. If a waiver participant is involved, the Administrator reviews SAF-08 for critical incident reporting.
The agency removes any suspected employee from contact with the client, and with all clients if needed, during the investigation. Removal is not discipline and is documented as such.
The agency cooperates fully with APS, law enforcement and DCH. It does not interfere with interviews or destroy or alter records.

The Administrator reviews each case for corrective action. This includes retraining, changes to staffing or schedules, and termination of employees found to have abused, neglected or exploited a client. The review is documented and trended in the QI program (GOV-04).
The agency does not retaliate against any employee, client or family member who makes a good-faith report. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination.
Staff who report in good faith are immune from civil and criminal liability under § 30-5-4(c). The agency tells all staff of this protection at orientation.
Reports, outcomes and follow-up are kept in the incident file for at least five years (.09(4)(d)).

responsibilities.duty: Report any reasonable cause to believe abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately, and call 911 if a client is in danger.
Makes or ensures reports to APS and law enforcement, removes suspected workers from contact, notifies responsible parties and case managers, keeps the file, and ensures corrective action.
Receive reports from caregivers without delay, make sure the Administrator is told at once, and keep the client safe.
Receives reports of confirmed cases and trends, and acts on any allegation involving the Administrator.

documentation: Signed applicant statements on abuse, neglect, exploitation and false statements
Background check and registry results
Orientation and annual training records on reporting
Incident file entry with report dates, times, agencies, intake numbers and outcome
Written reports sent after the initial report
Notifications to responsible party and case manager
Corrective action and QI documentation

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, supervisors, the Administrator and any contractor serving clients
policies.purpose: To make sure falls, accidents, significant medication errors and other unusual occurrences affecting client health, safety and welfare are reported, acted on, documented and reviewed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires every incident and unusual occurrence affecting a client's health, safety or welfare to be reported and documented. Examples are falls, accidents, injuries, significant medication errors, unexpected changes in condition, missing persons, property damage and allegations of misconduct. Incident reports and reports of unusual occurrences are kept for at least five years, and the documentation shows what actions the agency took (.09(4)(d)). Rule 111-8-65 sets no deadline for reporting incidents to DCH, so the agency applies an internal standard: the caregiver reports to the supervisor immediately, a written incident report is completed within 24 hours, and the Administrator reviews it within 2 business days. Handling of incidents is covered at orientation (.09(6)), and incidents are trended in the quality improvement program (.10(4)). Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported to APS and law enforcement under SAF-01.

definitions.definition: Any event that harms or could harm a client, caregiver or property, or that affects service delivery, such as a fall, accident, injury, medication error or sudden change in condition.
An event outside normal operations that affects client health, safety or welfare, even if no one was hurt.
A medication-related event that causes or could cause harm, such as taking the wrong medicine or dose, missing a critical dose, or a missed reminder that leads to a change in condition.
The agency's file of incident reports, with documentation of actions taken, kept for at least five years.

procedures: The caregiver makes sure the client is safe first. In an emergency the caregiver calls 911 and follows SAF-08 and SVC-08, and does not move an injured client unless the client is in immediate danger.

The caregiver reports the incident to the supervisor by phone immediately, and in any case before leaving the client's home, unless the caregiver is helping with an emergency. If the supervisor cannot be reached, the caregiver calls the agency's after-hours number or the Administrator.

The caregiver completes a written incident report within 24 hours, stating facts only: date, time, place, who was involved, what happened, what the client said, observed injuries, actions taken, and who was notified. Opinions and blame are left out.
The supervisor reviews the report on the day it is received, confirms the client is safe, and makes sure any needed medical care, follow-up or service plan change is arranged.

The supervisor or Administrator notifies the client's responsible party the same day, and notifies the physician and the waiver case manager or support coordinator when appropriate. The notification is documented with the date, time, person contacted and what was said.

If the incident involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Administrator follows SAF-01 and reports to APS and law enforcement. If the client is a waiver participant, the Administrator also checks whether SAF-08 requires a critical incident report.
The Administrator reviews each incident report within 2 business days, records findings and corrective actions on the report, and signs and dates it.
For a medication error, the supervisor follows SVC-05, verifies whether the client was harmed, and refers any clinical question to a nurse or the client's physician.
If a caregiver is injured, the supervisor ensures care and follows SAF-05. An employee illness or exposure goes through SAF-07.

The Administrator decides whether any other notice is needed, such as to the payer, an insurer or REC-02, and documents the decision. Because the rule sets no DCH reporting deadline, the Administrator reports to DCH if directed by DCH or if the Administrator considers the event significant.
The Billing Coordinator is told if an incident affects billing, for example a missed visit or an emergency departure (SVC-16).
Each incident report with actions taken is filed in the incident file and referenced in the client record (REC-01, REC-03). Reports are kept at least five years.

The QI Coordinator enters each incident in a log and reviews the log at least quarterly for patterns by client, caregiver, time and type. Findings and corrective actions are documented in the QI program (GOV-04).
Incident handling is covered at orientation before caregivers work with clients and is refreshed in annual in-service training (PER-03).
No employee is punished for reporting an incident or a mistake in good faith. Failure to report a known incident is a conduct violation (PER-07).

responsibilities.duty: Ensure client safety, report immediately by phone, and write the incident report within 24 hours.
Confirm client safety, notify the responsible party, physician and case manager as appropriate, and forward the report to the Administrator.
Reviews each incident within 2 business days, orders corrective action, decides on outside notices, and ensures five-year retention.
Logs incidents and reports trends quarterly.

documentation: Written incident reports with actions taken
Notification records (responsible party, physician, case manager)
Administrator review signature and date
Incident log and QI trend reports
Corrective action records
Orientation and in-service training records on incident handling

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, nurses (if offered), supervisors and the Administrator
federal: 29 CFR 1910.1030 (Bloodborne Pathogens), where employees have occupational exposure
policies.purpose: To reduce the spread of infection to clients and staff by training caregivers, supplying protective equipment, and keeping contagious employees from serving clients.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows infection prevention practices in every client home. The 40-hour personal care assistant program covers infection control in the home and home safety and sanitation (.09(5)(c)). Competency for companions and sitters includes infection control (.09(5)(d)). Orientation requires employees to report known exposure to tuberculosis or hepatitis to the agency (.09(6)). Supervisors do not knowingly permit an employee who has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis to serve clients until the employee is determined not to be contagious (.10(2)). Employee TB screening at hire and annually is a personnel record requirement (see PER-04 and PER-05). The agency provides gloves and other personal protective equipment (PPE). Standard precautions, including hand hygiene, glove use, and safe sharps and waste handling, are internal standards. The agency follows OSHA rules on bloodborne pathogens and PPE where employees have occupational exposure. Infection control is refreshed during the 8 hours of annual in-service training (.09(6)).

definitions.definition: Basic infection control practices used with every client, including hand hygiene, gloves, safe handling of soiled items, sharps and waste, and cleaning surfaces.
Personal protective equipment such as disposable gloves, masks, gowns and eye protection.
Contact with a person who has, or is suspected of having, TB, hepatitis or another communicable disease in a way that could spread infection, or contact with blood or body fluids.
Able to spread an infection to others. An employee is no longer contagious when a qualified clinician determines so.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a written infection control procedure covering hand hygiene, glove use, handling of soiled linen, cleaning and disinfecting, safe handling of sharps and waste, and respiratory hygiene.

Before caregivers work with clients, orientation covers this policy, standard precautions, the duty to report known exposure to TB or hepatitis, and the use and disposal of PPE (.09(6)). Completion is recorded in the personnel record.

Personal care assistants complete the infection control and home safety and sanitation content of the 40-hour training or an equivalent credential. Companions and sitters show competency in infection control. A supervisor documents competency by direct observation or demonstration (see PER-01 and PER-03).

The agency supplies caregivers with disposable gloves and other PPE at no cost, and replenishes supplies on request. A caregiver who has run out of PPE tells the supervisor immediately, and the supervisor delivers it or reschedules the task.
Caregivers wash hands before and after each client contact, before preparing food, after toileting or personal care tasks, after removing gloves and when visibly soiled.

Caregivers wear gloves for contact with blood, body fluids, wounds, soiled linens or items, and when assisting with toileting, perineal care or oral care. Gloves are changed between tasks and disposed of properly.
Caregivers do not perform sharps or wound tasks that are outside their scope. They report needle sticks, sharps found in the home and bloodied materials to the supervisor (SVC-01).
Caregivers bag soiled items and dispose of waste as instructed. They clean and disinfect shared surfaces and equipment after use.

A caregiver with symptoms of a contagious illness (for example fever, persistent cough, vomiting, diarrhea or a rash) tells the supervisor before the shift. The supervisor decides whether the caregiver may work and arranges coverage under SVC-06.

An employee who has been exposed to TB or hepatitis, or diagnosed with either, reports it to the Administrator immediately. The employee does not serve clients until a qualified clinician determines the employee is not contagious, and the Administrator keeps the clearance in the file (.10(2); see SAF-07).

The supervisor never knowingly allows an exposed or diagnosed employee to serve clients before clearance. If the supervisor learns of an exposure, the supervisor removes the employee from the schedule the same day and tells the Administrator.
The Administrator ensures TB screening is completed at hire and annually and that results are filed (PER-04, PER-05).

If a client has a known or suspected contagious condition, the supervisor tells the caregivers who need to know, within confidentiality limits (CR-03), makes sure they have the right PPE and precautions, and may consult a nurse or the client's physician (SVC-13).
After a caregiver is exposed to blood or body fluids, the caregiver washes the area, tells the supervisor immediately and follows SAF-07. The agency documents the event as an incident (SAF-02).
Infection control practice is observed during the annual written evaluation and supervisory visits (SVC-04, PER-09). Gaps lead to retraining.
The agency includes infection control in the 8 clock hours of annual in-service training and keeps the sign-in sheets.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains infection control procedures, provides PPE, ensures training and TB screening, and decides on work restrictions with clinical input.
Observe infection control practice, keep contagious employees off the schedule until cleared, and arrange PPE and coverage.
Use standard precautions, wear PPE, report symptoms and exposures, and follow work restrictions.
Advises on infection risks for medically frail clients and on exposure follow-up.

documentation: Written infection control procedure
Orientation and competency records showing infection control
Annual in-service sign-in sheets
TB screening records at hire and annually
Exposure reports and clearance documentation
PPE supply log
Incident reports for exposures

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, scheduling staff and all caregivers
federal: 42 CFR 441.301(c) (waiver plan of care risk planning, where applicable)
policies.purpose: To prepare clients and staff for medical emergencies, severe weather, power outages and evacuations, and to make sure the most vulnerable clients are contacted first.
policies.policy: Rule 111-8-65 has no emergency preparedness or disaster plan requirement for private home care providers, so this policy is an internal standard and good practice. [AGENCY NAME] confirms any waiver-specific requirements with DAS and DBHDD. The policy builds on requirements that do exist: orientation covers handling medical emergencies and incidents (.09(6)); companion and sitter competency includes handling medical emergencies in the home (.09(5)(d)); and a provider representative must be on call and able to reach a nurse supervisor when caregivers provide personal care to medically frail or compromised clients (.10(2)(d)). Emergency information is recorded in the service plan (.11). The agency assigns each client a risk tier at intake, plans for severe weather, outages and evacuation, contacts the most medically vulnerable clients first, keeps an after-hours number and an agency continuity plan, and tests the plan at least annually.
