definitions.definition: A rating of a client's vulnerability in an emergency, based on factors such as oxygen or power-dependent equipment, mobility limits, cognitive impairment and lack of a caregiver backup.
A client whose medical condition makes them especially vulnerable if services are interrupted. See SVC-13.
The agency's plan for keeping staffing, records access, communication and client contact going during an emergency.
Contacting the highest-risk clients first when an emergency or disaster occurs.

procedures: At intake, the intake staff member asks about oxygen or other power-dependent equipment, mobility limits, cognitive impairment, whether the client lives alone, the availability of family or other caregiver backup, and special diet or medication needs (SVC-02).

The supervisor assigns a risk tier (for example high, moderate or standard) using those factors and records it in the client record. Any client who uses oxygen or power-dependent equipment, has significant mobility limits or cognitive impairment, or has no backup caregiver is placed in the high tier.

The supervisor records the emergency plan in the service plan (.11): emergency contacts, physician, preferred hospital, medications and equipment, evacuation needs, where the client would go, and the participant's own choices. For waiver clients the plan is consistent with the plan of care from the case manager or support coordinator.

The Scheduling Coordinator keeps a current list of all clients by risk tier with phone numbers and emergency contacts, available outside the office, for example in a secure cloud system, and updates it at least monthly and when a plan changes.

At orientation, before they work with clients, caregivers are trained on how to recognize and respond to a medical emergency, when to call 911, how to report an emergency and incident to the agency, and what to do in the home during fire, severe weather or loss of power (.09(6); .09(5)(d)). The training is recorded.

In a medical emergency the caregiver calls 911, stays with the client, gives basic help within training, calls the supervisor or the after-hours number, and completes an incident report (SVC-08, SAF-02).

The Administrator designates an on-call provider representative every day, including nights and weekends, who can be reached by phone. For medically frail or compromised clients, the representative must be able to reach a nurse supervisor by phone or other means to consult with staff on the clients' medical needs (.10(2)(d); SVC-13).
The agency keeps a working after-hours phone number, gives it to every client and caregiver at intake or hire, and tests it at least quarterly.

When severe weather or another disaster is forecast or occurs, the Administrator or on-call representative activates the continuity plan. This covers deciding which visits can safely proceed, telling caregivers, and checking on clients.

Priority outreach starts with high-tier clients, especially those on oxygen or power-dependent equipment. Staff call, record the result and escalate to emergency contacts, 911 or a welfare check if a client cannot be reached and may be at risk. Moderate and standard-tier clients are contacted next.

Caregivers are never required to enter unsafe conditions. A caregiver who cannot reach a client safely tells the supervisor, and the supervisor arranges another approach such as a phone check, a family member or a welfare check (SAF-05).
If a visit is missed or delayed because of an emergency, the agency follows SVC-06 and SVC-12 to notify the client and arrange other coverage.

The agency's continuity plan covers how staff reach each other if phones or power are down, how the schedule and client records are accessed if the office is closed, who makes decisions, and how clients, responsible parties and case managers are told about changes in service.
After any real emergency, the Administrator holds a review within 14 days, documents lessons learned and updates the plan (GOV-04).

The Administrator tests the plan at least annually, through a drill or tabletop exercise that includes a priority outreach call, an after-hours call test and a records access test. Results and corrections are documented.
Emergency and disaster procedures are reviewed with caregivers during annual in-service training (PER-03), and with clients and responsible parties at the service plan review (SVC-03).

responsibilities.duty: Owns the plan, designates the on-call representative, activates the continuity plan, tests it annually and reviews after real events.
Assign risk tiers, record emergency plans in the service plan, and carry out priority outreach to clients.
Maintains the client list by risk tier and the after-hours number, and manages schedule changes in an emergency.
Answers calls, supports caregivers, and reaches a nurse supervisor for medically frail clients.
Call 911 for emergencies, follow the emergency plan, report to the agency and put their own safety first.

documentation: Risk tier assigned at intake
Emergency plan in the service plan
Client list by risk tier and emergency contacts
On-call schedule and after-hours number test log
Orientation and in-service training records on emergencies
Incident reports for emergencies
Priority outreach logs
Annual test results and post-event reviews

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All employees who work in client homes, including personal care assistants, companions/sitters, nurses and supervisors, and the administrator.
policies.purpose: To protect caregivers from injury, assault and unsafe conditions while working in client homes, and to make sure staff know they may leave an unsafe situation without penalty.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will provide a workplace free from recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious harm. Rule 111-8-65 has no separate workplace violence provision. This policy rests on two rule requirements. Home safety and ambulation and transfer are required topics of the 40-hour personal care assistant training under Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(c). Annual training on subjects related to each employee's duties is required under Rule 111-8-65-.09(6). Every client is screened for safety hazards at intake. Caregivers may leave an unsafe situation and must call their supervisor. All injuries and assaults are reported the same day. No employee will be disciplined or retaliated against for refusing unsafe work in good faith.

definitions.definition: Any physical assault, threat of physical harm, harassment or intimidating behavior directed at an employee by a client, family member, visitor, co-worker or other person while the employee is working.

A review at intake of known risks in the home and surroundings, including weapons, aggressive behavior, pets, environmental hazards and an unsafe neighborhood, completed before the first caregiver visit.

Any condition in which a reasonable person would believe there is an immediate risk of injury, assault or serious harm, including violence, threats, impairment, weapons displayed, severe hazards or unsafe animals.
Body mechanics and assistive device use taught during ambulation and transfer training to reduce the risk of injury to the caregiver and the client.

procedures: During intake (SVC-02), the intake coordinator or supervising nurse completes the Home Safety and Caregiver Risk Screening. It covers weapons in the home, history of aggression or threats, household members with known behavioral concerns, pets, smoking and oxygen use, clutter, pests, lighting, stairs, lack of working utilities, and neighborhood safety.

The supervisor reviews the screening results before the first visit and documents controls, such as a two-person first visit, daytime-only scheduling, securing pets, a safety call-in or check-in, or a refusal to serve if risks cannot be controlled.
Caregivers receive the relevant risk information in the service plan or assignment sheet before the first visit.
Orientation (PER-03) includes caregiver safety and workplace violence content: recognizing escalation, de-escalation, personal safety in client homes and parking areas, and how to leave a situation.

Training for personal care assistants includes home safety, ambulation and transfer, and safe lifting under the required 40-hour curriculum. The agency also provides refresher training on safe lifting and transfer as part of the 8 hours of annual training required for each employee after the first year of employment.

Caregivers use safe lifting and transfer technique and any assistive devices (gait belt, mechanical lift, slide sheet) identified in the service plan. A caregiver must not attempt a transfer he or she has not been trained and found competent to perform, and must not attempt a lift that appears unsafe.
Caregivers use personal protective equipment as directed in SAF-03 and SAF-07.

If a caregiver feels unsafe at any point, including because of threats, weapons, intoxicated or violent persons, aggressive animals or hazardous conditions, the caregiver may leave immediately. When it is safe to do so, the caregiver calls 911 if there is an immediate danger and then calls the supervisor or on-call line at [PHONE].

If the client cannot safely be left alone, the caregiver stays in a safe location until the supervisor arranges a replacement or contacts emergency services, and does not leave the client in an emergency.
The supervisor contacts the client or responsible party, arranges alternate coverage if appropriate and starts any needed notices under SAF-01, SAF-02 and SVC-08.

The caregiver reports every injury, assault, threat or near-miss to the supervisor on the same day. The supervisor completes an incident report (SAF-02) and, for injuries, the workers' compensation first report of injury.

The administrator makes sure injured employees are offered medical evaluation and that workers' compensation coverage is in force. The administrator confirms coverage requirements under Georgia law with the agency's insurance broker. The carrier is [WORKERS' COMPENSATION CARRIER].

Within 7 days of any assault or serious injury, the administrator reviews the event with the supervisor and the employee, decides whether the client's services can continue safely, and documents the decision and any corrective action.
If the agency decides that services cannot be provided safely, the administrator follows SVC-09 for discharge or transfer and SVC-12 for client referral.
No employee will be disciplined, have hours reduced or be retaliated against for refusing unsafe work in good faith, for leaving an unsafe situation or for reporting a safety concern.
The administrator reviews injury, assault and near-miss trends at least quarterly and reports them to the QA/PI process (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Provides resources, training and workers' compensation coverage; reviews serious events and trends; enforces the no-retaliation rule.
Completes and reviews pre-visit safety screening, communicates risks to caregivers, responds to caregiver calls and completes incident reports.
Follows safe work practices, uses safe lifting techniques, leaves unsafe situations, calls the supervisor and reports injuries or threats the same day.

documentation: Home Safety and Caregiver Risk Screening in the client record
Incident reports and workers' compensation first reports of injury
Training records for orientation, safe lifting and annual in-service in the personnel record
Administrator review notes and QA/PI trend summaries

policies.title: Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: All caregivers and supervisors who accompany, drive or arrange transportation for clients.
policies.purpose: To make sure transport and escort services are provided only with the required client authorization and insurance protections, and in a safe manner.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides transport and escort services as defined in Rule 111-8-65-.03(s): accompanying a client, or providing or arranging transportation, to places outside the residence such as appointments, shopping, recreation and social activities. If an employee drives a vehicle not owned by the client, the agency will either obtain the client's signed waiver of claims for damages from operation of the vehicle or make reasonable efforts to confirm current motor vehicle insurance with medical coverage for the client. The waiver or proof is kept in the client file. If the client's own vehicle will be used, approval is documented in the service agreement. Only caregivers who have completed competency evaluation in transport and escort, and who meet the agency's driver standards, may drive clients.

definitions.definition: Accompanying a client, or providing or arranging transportation, to places outside the residence, such as medical appointments, shopping, recreation and social activities.

A written statement signed by the client releasing the agency and employee from claims for damages arising from operation of the vehicle, used when an employee drives a vehicle not owned by the client.
Commercial liability coverage that protects the agency when employees use their own or other non-agency vehicles on agency business.

procedures: At intake (SVC-02), the intake coordinator asks whether the client needs or wants transport and escort and records the types of trips, frequency and who will drive.

The service agreement, under Rule 111-8-65-.09(2)(a), states whether transport is included and records the client's approval for use of the client's motor vehicle if that vehicle will be used. The agreement is completed by the 2nd visit if on a different day than the 1st, or within 7 calendar days of first service, whichever is earlier.

If an employee will drive a vehicle not owned by the client (the employee's vehicle or an agency vehicle), before the first trip the supervisor either obtains the client's signed waiver of claims, or makes and documents reasonable efforts to confirm current motor vehicle insurance with medical coverage for the client.
The supervisor files the signed waiver or the proof of insurance and the notes on the efforts made in the client record before the first trip.

Only caregivers whose competency evaluation includes transport and escort services, as required for companions/sitters under Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(d), may drive or escort clients. The supervisor verifies this before assignment.

Before authorizing a caregiver to drive clients, the administrator verifies a valid driver's license, a satisfactory motor vehicle record check, proof of the employee's current automobile liability insurance, and a vehicle in safe operating condition. These are internal standards and the proof is kept in the personnel record.
The administrator maintains hired and non-owned auto liability coverage for the agency and reviews it at least annually with the insurance broker.
Before each trip the caregiver confirms the destination, expected return time and any client needs (wheelchair, walker, oxygen) and confirms the trip is within the service plan.

The caregiver makes sure the client and the caregiver wear seat belts at all times. The caregiver does not use a handheld phone, text or drive while impaired, and does not drive the client if feeling unfit to drive.

Caregivers do not lift or perform physical transfers into or out of a vehicle that they have not been trained and found competent to perform. If a transfer cannot be done safely, the caregiver does not attempt it and calls the supervisor.
Caregivers do not transport persons other than the client unless the supervisor has approved it and it is safe, and do not make personal stops or accept payment for rides.

The caregiver records mileage, destination and times for each trip on the visit record or mileage log and has the client or responsible party initial it when practical. Mileage is reimbursed under the agency's wage and expense procedures (PER-06).

If an accident, injury, breakdown or other incident occurs during transport, the caregiver calls 911 if needed, ensures the client's safety, notifies the supervisor immediately and completes an incident report under SAF-02. The supervisor notifies the responsible party and any waiver case manager as required.
The supervisor reviews the mileage log, waiver and insurance documentation at each supervisory visit and the administrator reviews driver files at least annually.
If a client's vehicle is used, the caregiver uses it only for the trips approved in the service agreement and returns it with the keys to the client.

responsibilities.duty: Approves driver standards, maintains hired and non-owned auto coverage and reviews driver files annually.
Obtains the waiver or insurance proof before the first trip, verifies caregiver competency, reviews mileage logs and responds to transport incidents.
Maintains a valid license and insurance, drives safely, uses seat belts, keeps the mileage log and reports incidents immediately.
Signs the waiver or approves use of the client's vehicle in the service agreement, as applicable.

documentation: Service agreement showing transport services and vehicle authorization
Client's signed waiver of claims, or proof and notes of efforts to confirm vehicle insurance with medical coverage
Driver's license, motor vehicle record and insurance proof in the personnel record
Competency evaluation covering transport and escort
Mileage logs and trip records
Incident reports for transport events

policies.title: Employee Exposure to TB, Hepatitis and Bloodborne Pathogens — Work Restrictions
policies.applies_to: All employees, supervisors and the administrator.
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of tuberculosis, hepatitis and bloodborne pathogens between employees and clients, and to make sure exposed or infected employees are removed from client contact until it is safe.
policies.policy: Employees must report to [AGENCY NAME] any known exposure to tuberculosis (TB) or hepatitis, as taught in orientation under Rule 111-8-65-.09(6). No supervisor will knowingly allow an employee who has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis to serve clients until it is determined that the employee is not contagious, as required by Rule 111-8-65-.10(2). The determination must come from a health care provider and be documented. TB screening is required at hire and annually, and the results are kept in the personnel record under Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(c). Where employees have reasonably anticipated occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials, the agency complies with the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard. Exposure and medical records are confidential and kept separately from the personnel file.

definitions.definition: Close contact with a person who has active TB or hepatitis, or contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials through needlestick, cut, splash to mucous membranes or non-intact skin.
Able to transmit an infectious disease to others, as determined by a health care provider.
A written plan identifying job tasks with occupational exposure and the controls, training, vaccination and post-exposure follow-up the agency uses to protect employees.
A record of percutaneous injuries from contaminated sharps, kept to identify and reduce exposure risks.

procedures: During orientation (PER-03), every employee is trained on the duty to report any known exposure to TB or hepatitis, and on the agency's exposure control procedures. The employee signs an acknowledgment.

Before working with clients, each employee has a satisfactory TB screening, and the screening is repeated annually. The supervisor tracks due dates and the result is kept in the personnel record (PER-04, PER-05).
An employee who has been exposed to TB or hepatitis, has symptoms or has been diagnosed with either illness must notify the supervisor immediately, before the next scheduled visit.
The supervisor removes the employee from client contact right away, arranges replacement coverage under SVC-06 and does not allow the employee to return on the basis of self-report alone.

The employee is referred to a health care provider for evaluation. The employee returns to client contact only after the provider documents that the employee is not contagious and the supervisor has reviewed the written clearance.
The supervisor places the written clearance, with dates of removal and return, in the confidential medical file.

If a client may have been exposed, the administrator consults the local health department or the employee's health care provider as appropriate and notifies affected clients or responsible parties as advised. Notice is documented, and privacy is protected under CR-03.
For employees with reasonably anticipated occupational exposure, the administrator keeps a written exposure control plan, reviews it at least annually and updates it when tasks or procedures change.

The agency offers the hepatitis B vaccine series at no cost to employees with occupational exposure within 10 working days of initial assignment, unless the employee declines in writing, previously received it or has immunity.
The agency provides personal protective equipment (gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection), sharps containers and cleaning supplies, and trains employees in their use under SAF-03.

After a needlestick, splash or other exposure to blood or body fluids, the employee immediately washes the site or flushes the area, reports to the supervisor the same day, and is offered a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up at no cost.
The supervisor documents the circumstances of the exposure, including the route, the task being done and the source individual if known, and completes an incident report under SAF-02.
The administrator records any sharps injury in the sharps injury log, without employee identification in the log, and reviews the cause to prevent recurrence.

Exposure incident records, vaccination records, medical evaluations and clearances are kept in a confidential medical file, separate from the personnel file, and released only as allowed by law. The agency retains them as required by OSHA and law.
Employees must not be penalized for reporting an exposure or illness. The administrator reviews exposure events and work-restriction cases at least quarterly in QA/PI (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the exposure control plan, vaccine program and supplies; ensures work restrictions are enforced; keeps confidential medical files.
Removes exposed or diagnosed employees from client contact, tracks TB screening, obtains clearance and arranges coverage.
Reports known exposures and symptoms immediately, completes TB screening, uses PPE and does not return to client contact without written clearance.

documentation: TB screening results at hire and annually (personnel record)
Orientation acknowledgment of the duty to report exposure
Health care provider clearance and dates of work restriction (confidential medical file)
Exposure incident reports and post-exposure follow-up records
Hepatitis B vaccine offer, acceptance or declination
Written exposure control plan and sharps injury log

policies.title: Waiver Critical Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees who serve, supervise or manage services for clients in the CCSP/SOURCE (Elderly and Disabled Waiver), ICWP and NOW/COMP waiver programs.
policies.purpose: To make sure serious events affecting waiver clients are promptly reported to the case manager or support coordinator and the waiver program, documented and followed up, in support of the health and welfare assurance required of Medicaid waiver services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] serves waiver clients under the Georgia Elderly and Disabled Waiver (CCSP/SOURCE), a 1915(c) waiver whose reimbursement, enrollment and utilization review are handled by DCH and whose day-to-day CCSP operations are run by the Division of Aging Services, and under the ICWP and NOW/COMP waivers. CCSP in-home service providers must hold a current, valid DCH private home care license. Waiver critical incident categories, reporting methods and deadlines are set by the waiver programs, and the agency follows the versions in the current DAS HCBS manual and the current DBHDD provider manual. The administrator keeps a Critical Incident Reference Sheet containing those categories and deadlines, and no waiver client may be served until it is in place. Nothing in this policy extends a program deadline. The agency notifies the case manager or support coordinator of serious events including injury, hospitalization, abuse, neglect, exploitation, death and a missing person. All incidents are also documented and retained for at least five years under Rule 111-8-65-.09(4)(d).

definitions.definition: A serious event involving a waiver client that the waiver program requires to be reported, including at minimum injury, hospitalization, abuse, neglect, exploitation, death and a missing person, as further defined in the program manuals.
The waiver program staff person responsible for the client's plan of care, such as the CCSP/SOURCE case manager or the ICWP or NOW/COMP support coordinator.

The agency's one-page reference listing each waiver program's current reportable incident categories, who must be notified, how, and by what deadline, taken from the current DAS HCBS manual and DBHDD provider manual.
A client whose whereabouts are unknown when he or she is expected to be at home or in the caregiver's presence, and who cannot be located after reasonable efforts.

procedures: The administrator obtains the current DAS HCBS manual and DBHDD provider manual before the agency serves any waiver client. From them the administrator builds the Critical Incident Reference Sheet for each waiver program the agency serves, listing categories, notification recipients, methods and deadlines.
The administrator reviews the Reference Sheet against the current manuals at least annually and whenever a program issues a policy change. Each version is dated and previous versions are kept.
Critical incident reporting is covered in orientation and annual training (PER-03). Each caregiver receives the Reference Sheet and the supervisor's and on-call phone number [PHONE].

A caregiver who witnesses or learns of a serious event, such as injury, hospitalization, suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, death, or a missing person, first protects the client's safety and calls 911 if there is an emergency (SVC-08).
The caregiver notifies the supervisor immediately by phone, and in any case before the end of the shift, and gives a written account on the incident form the same day.

The supervisor decides at once whether the event meets a critical incident category on the Reference Sheet. If unsure, the supervisor treats it as reportable and contacts the case manager or support coordinator for guidance.
Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is also reported through the mandatory reporting channels in SAF-01, in addition to waiver reporting.

The supervisor notifies the client's case manager or support coordinator, and any other recipient listed on the Reference Sheet, within the program deadline. Our internal target is verbal notice the same day the agency learns of the event, with written follow-up by the deadline on the Reference Sheet.
The supervisor notifies the administrator immediately of every critical incident. The administrator reviews and approves each waiver report before or immediately after it is sent.
The supervisor informs the client's representative or family, unless the representative is the suspected perpetrator or the case manager advises otherwise, and documents the contact.
The agency cooperates with any investigation by the waiver program, DCH, DAS, DBHDD or law enforcement and supplies requested records consistent with CR-03 and REC-04.

The supervisor completes a corrective action and follow-up plan for each critical incident, such as a plan update (SVC-03), added supervision, staff retraining or changes in assignment, and documents the date and person responsible.
If an employee is involved in the incident, the administrator decides whether to remove the employee from client contact pending review, and documents the decision.
Every incident, whether or not it is a reportable critical incident, is documented on an incident report under SAF-02 and kept in the complaint and incident file for at least five years (REC-03).

The administrator logs all waiver critical incidents, including dates reported and notified, and reviews the log at least quarterly in QA/PI (GOV-04) for trends, late reports and prevention opportunities.
Billing for the affected client is reviewed by the administrator under SVC-16 when an incident affects service delivery, such as a hospitalization or a missed visit.

responsibilities.duty: Builds and updates the Critical Incident Reference Sheet from current program manuals, approves waiver reports, keeps the log and leads QA/PI review.
Determines reportability, notifies the case manager or support coordinator and the client representative, and completes follow-up plans.
Protects the client, calls 911 when needed, reports to the supervisor immediately and completes the incident form the same day.

documentation: Critical Incident Reference Sheet with dated versions
Incident reports and written accounts from caregivers
Copies of waiver critical incident notices and confirmations of notice to case managers or support coordinators
Record of notice to client representatives
Corrective action and follow-up documentation
Critical incident log and QA/PI review notes, retained at least five years

policies.title: Caregiver Qualifications and Credentials (PCA, Companion/Sitter, Nurse)
policies.applies_to: All applicants and employees in the roles of personal care assistant (PCA), companion/sitter and nurse, and the supervisors who assign them.
federal: 42 CFR Part 483 Subpart D (nurse aide training and competency programs, referenced by Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(c))
policies.purpose: To make sure every caregiver meets the qualifications Georgia requires for the tasks he or she will perform, and that proof of qualification is verified and kept.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will keep sufficient qualified staff for its service agreements and will assign tasks only to employees who are qualified for them. Georgia has no separate state registry or certification for private home care provider aides, so the agency verifies each qualification itself. A PCA must satisfy at least one route in Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(c): a nurse aide program under 42 CFR Part 483 Subpart D, a DCH-recognized nurse aide competency exam, a DCH-approved health care or personal care credential, or the agency's 40-hour training program. A companion/sitter may perform only companion or sitter tasks unless also qualified as a nurse or PCA, and must meet Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(d). Nursing personnel must hold a Georgia license, as required by Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(b). All hires must have no credible evidence of abuse or exploitation, must complete orientation and training, and must make no false statements about qualifications, as required by Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(a). No PCA will be assigned a task without completed training and a competency determination, and no PCA will care for a client with special conditions without training and demonstrated competency.

definitions.definition: An employee qualified under Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(c) to perform personal care tasks and the other tasks for which training and competency are documented.
An employee who performs only companion or sitter tasks, unless also qualified as a nurse or PCA.

The agency's PCA training program covering ambulation and transfer, personal care tasks, first aid and CPR, special conditions, home management, home safety and sanitation, infection control, medically related activities and vital signs, and nutrition, directed by a registered nurse or an equivalent professional.
A written evaluation by direct observation or demonstration that the employee can safely perform an assigned task.
Client conditions that require specific training and demonstrated competency before a PCA may provide care.

procedures: The administrator or designee defines the job description for each role (PCA, companion/sitter, nurse) listing the tasks the role may and may not perform, consistent with SVC-01.

At application, each applicant signs a statement that he or she has no credible evidence of abuse or exploitation and that all information given about qualifications is true. Any false statement disqualifies the applicant (see PER-02).

For a PCA applicant, the supervisor identifies which qualifying route applies: nurse aide training and competency program under 42 CFR Part 483 Subpart D; DCH-recognized nurse aide competency exam; DCH-recognized health care or personal care credential; or the agency's 40-hour training program.

For applicants claiming a nurse aide credential, the supervisor verifies it through the Georgia Nurse Aide Registry or the issuing program, and for other credentials obtains the certificate or transcript and verifies it with the issuer. Copies are placed in the personnel record.

For applicants who will complete the agency's 40-hour program, the registered nurse or equivalent professional directing the program documents attendance and content for each topic: ambulation and transfer, personal care tasks, first aid and CPR, special conditions, home management, home safety and sanitation, infection control, vital signs and medically related activities, and nutrition.

Twenty hours of the 40-hour program must be completed before the PCA serves any client. The remaining 20 hours must be completed within six months of the start date. The supervisor tracks the six-month deadline and does not schedule the PCA for unsupervised work beyond what the completed training supports.

The program director completes a written competency evaluation by direct observation or demonstration for each task before the PCA is assigned that task. The supervisor files the evaluation in the personnel record.

Before assigning a PCA to a client with special conditions, the supervisor verifies that the PCA has been trained on that condition and has demonstrated competency, and documents this in the assignment.

For a companion/sitter, the supervisor confirms that the person can read, write, follow instructions and complete reports (through a reading and writing exercise at interview). The supervisor also confirms training or competency in the needs of elderly, handicapped or convalescing persons, meal preparation, transport and escort, housekeeping and sanitation, home safety, handling medical emergencies and infection control.

A companion/sitter is assigned only companion or sitter tasks unless the person also meets PCA or nurse qualifications. The supervisor makes sure the service plan and caregiver assignment sheet reflect this limit.

For a nurse, the administrator verifies the Georgia license directly with the licensing board at hire, confirms it is active and without restriction, and records the license number and expiration date. Verification is repeated at each renewal, and at least annually.
The supervisor confirms that each new hire completes orientation and training under PER-03 before working with clients.
The supervisor keeps proof of every qualification and competency evaluation in the personnel record (PER-05).
The scheduler checks qualifications against the assignment before any caregiver is placed with a client. No caregiver is assigned a task outside the caregiver's documented qualifications.

The administrator audits all caregiver qualification files at least annually and when a license, credential or training deadline is due. Gaps are corrected immediately by removing the caregiver from the affected tasks until resolved.
The administrator maintains a staffing roster showing the role, qualification route, credential expiration and training completion dates of each caregiver.

responsibilities.duty: Sets qualification standards, verifies nurse licenses, audits files annually and ensures sufficient qualified staff.
Verifies credentials, directs the 40-hour program, performs competency evaluations and assigns tasks only within documented qualifications.
Assigns caregivers only to tasks and clients for which they are qualified.
Provides truthful qualification information, completes required training, and performs only the tasks he or she is qualified for.

documentation: Application and signed statement of no credible evidence of abuse or exploitation and no false statements
Proof of credential: certificate, registry verification, transcript or license verification
40-hour training attendance and content records with 20-hour and six-month completion dates
Written competency evaluations by direct observation or demonstration
Training and competency records for special conditions
Nurse license verification and renewal dates
Staffing and qualification roster

policies.title: Background Checks and Employee Registries
policies.applies_to: Owners, the administrator, all applicants and employees, and contractors who have client contact.
federal: 42 USC 1320a-7 and 42 CFR Part 1001 (OIG exclusion), for Medicaid providers
42 CFR 483.156 (nurse aide registry, where a CNA credential is used)
policies.purpose: To protect clients by making sure owners, the administrator and caregivers have been screened, are not excluded from Medicaid and have no credible evidence of abuse, neglect or exploitation, before they have client contact.
policies.policy: The owner must comply with the Criminal Background Checks rules (Chapter 111-8-12) before a new private home care license is issued, as required by Rule 111-8-65-.05(1)(b). The administrator must have no credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation, and the current text of Rule 111-8-65-.09(3)(a)1 also calls for a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination. At application, every employee must give a statement that he or she has never been shown by credible evidence to have abused, neglected, sexually assaulted, exploited or deprived any person, as required by Rule 111-8-65-.09(5)(a). DCH may require additional verification of the qualifications of the administrator and employees at any time under Rule 111-8-65-.05(2). Which positions beyond the owner and administrator are covered by Chapter 111-8-12 has not been confirmed, so the administrator will confirm the current requirement with the DCH Healthcare Facility Regulation Division (HFRD) and follow it. As an internal standard, [AGENCY NAME] will also obtain a fingerprint-based records check for every employee with client contact, and will check exclusion lists and registries before hire and monthly for Medicaid-billing staff. No one will be assigned to client contact until all checks have cleared.

definitions.definition: A written determination, issued through the process designated under Chapter 111-8-12, that the person's fingerprint-based criminal history does not disqualify the person.
Reliable information, such as a substantiated finding or an adjudication, showing that a person abused, neglected, sexually assaulted, exploited or deprived another person.
The List of Excluded Individuals and Entities maintained by the HHS Office of Inspector General. Persons on it may not be employed in roles paid by federal health care programs.
The state registry of certified nurse aides, which shows certification status and any substantiated findings of abuse, neglect or misappropriation.
Any in-person or remote contact with clients or access to client homes, funds or records in the course of work.

procedures: Before submitting a new license application, each owner completes the background check process required under Chapter 111-8-12. The administrator keeps the owner's satisfactory determination in the license file and does not begin services until the license or provisional license is issued under Rule 111-8-65-.05.

Before appointment, the administrator candidate completes the criminal background check process, and the governing body confirms a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination, a statement of no credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation, and no false statements in the application (GOV-01, PER-08).

At least once a year and whenever the rules change, the administrator contacts HFRD to confirm which positions beyond the owner and administrator are covered by Chapter 111-8-12 and records the date, person spoken to and answer in the compliance file.

Each applicant completes an application and signs the statement that he or she has never been shown by credible evidence to have abused, neglected, sexually assaulted, exploited or deprived any person, and that all information is true. Where the answer is oral, the interviewer records it in writing and signs it.

For every employee who will have client contact, the agency obtains a fingerprint-based records check through the process designated under Chapter 111-8-12 and receives a satisfactory determination. This is an internal standard.

Before any client contact, the administrator or designee checks and documents the HHS OIG LEIE, the Georgia Medicaid exclusion list, the sex offender registry, and for any caregiver using a CNA credential, the Georgia Nurse Aide Registry. Each result is printed or saved with the date and the name of the person who checked.
The administrator repeats the exclusion list and registry checks monthly for all staff who may be involved in Medicaid-billed services, and records each monthly check on the exclusion check log.

The agency does not hire, assign or retain any person who is excluded from federal health care programs, who has a substantiated finding on the nurse aide registry, who is listed on the sex offender registry, or for whom there is credible evidence of abuse, neglect, sexual assault, exploitation or deprivation.

Where a records check shows a record or a result that is not clearly satisfactory, the administrator holds the applicant out of client contact, reviews the finding against the Chapter 111-8-12 standards and consults HFRD if needed. The decision and reasons are documented.

The administrator verifies each applicant's stated qualifications and employment history under PER-01 and PER-05. A false statement about qualifications or history is grounds for rejecting the applicant or for termination.

Employees must tell the administrator within 24 hours if they are arrested for, charged with or convicted of an offense, are named in an abuse, neglect or exploitation investigation, or are excluded or sanctioned. The administrator reviews and may remove the employee from client contact pending the outcome.

If the agency becomes aware of an employee's exclusion, a substantiated finding or credible evidence of abuse, neglect or exploitation, the administrator immediately removes the person from client contact and reports as required under SAF-01, GOV-05 and REC-02.

The administrator responds to any request from DCH for additional verification of the qualifications of the administrator or employees (Rule 111-8-65-.05(2)) promptly and supplies the records requested.
The agency does not assign a new hire to any client until the signed statement is on file, all checks have cleared and the scheduler has confirmed clearance in writing.

Background check results, determinations and exclusion logs are kept as confidential records, are accessible only to the administrator and designated staff, and are not shared except as required by law. They are filed per PER-05.
The administrator audits background and exclusion check documentation for all staff at least quarterly and reports results in QA/PI (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Completes owner checks before licensure and confirms the administrator's satisfactory determination before appointment.
Confirms applicable requirements with HFRD, ensures all checks are complete and logged, runs monthly exclusion checks and removes ineligible persons from client contact.
Assigns no one to client contact without written clearance.
Gives truthful statements and reports arrests, charges, convictions, investigations and exclusions within 24 hours.

documentation: Owner and administrator records check determinations
Signed applicant statements about abuse, neglect, exploitation and deprivation, and truthfulness
Fingerprint records check determinations for employees
OIG LEIE, Georgia Medicaid exclusion, sex offender registry and Nurse Aide Registry results with dates and checker names
Monthly exclusion check log
Record of HFRD contact on covered positions
Review decisions where a result is not clearly satisfactory

policies.title: Orientation, Competency Evaluation and Annual Training
policies.applies_to: All employees and contractors who provide client services (Personal Care Assistants, companions/sitters, nurses) and their supervisors
policies.purpose: To make sure every caregiver is oriented before working with clients, is trained and found competent before being assigned any task, and receives ongoing training, as Georgia Rule 111-8-65 requires of a Private Home Care Provider.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not allow any employee to work with a client until orientation is complete. No Personal Care Assistant (PCA) is assigned a personal care task until required training is finished and a supervisor has determined competency. No PCA cares for a client with a special condition without specific training and demonstrated competency. Companions/sitters perform only companion or sitter tasks unless they are also qualified as a PCA or nurse. Every employee receives at least 8 clock hours of in-service training each year after the first year of employment, on subjects related to the employee's duties. Every employee is evaluated in writing by a qualified supervisor, by direct observation or demonstration, at least annually. All orientation, training and competency records are kept in the employee's personnel record.

definitions.definition: Training completed before an employee works with any client, covering the topics listed in this policy.
A written finding by a qualified supervisor, based on direct observation or demonstration, that an employee can safely and correctly perform a specific task.
Sixty minutes of actual instruction or supervised practice, excluding breaks and meals.
A client diagnosis or need (for example, dementia, mobility limitation or a medical device) that requires specific training and demonstrated competency before a PCA may provide care.
A person designated under PER-08 who is qualified by education, training and experience to supervise the services being evaluated.

procedures: Before the first client contact, the Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) or designated supervisor gives each new employee orientation and records the date, hours, trainer name and employee signature on the orientation checklist.

Orientation covers, at minimum: (a) this agency's written policies on scope of services and the types of clients served; (b) client rights, responsibilities and the complaint process; (c) the employee's specific duties and job description; (d) how to report client progress and problems, and how to handle medical emergencies and incidents; and (e) the employee's duty to report known exposure to tuberculosis (TB) or hepatitis.
The new employee signs a statement acknowledging receipt of the job description and the policies covered in orientation. The statement is filed in the personnel record.

For each PCA hire, the supervisor first checks whether the employee holds a qualifying credential: completion of a nurse aide program under 42 CFR Part 483 Subpart D, a DCH-recognized nurse aide competency exam, or a DCH-approved health care or personal care credential. A copy of the credential is verified and filed (see PER-01).

A PCA without a qualifying credential must complete the agency's 40-hour training program. It is directed by a registered nurse or an equivalent professional and covers ambulation and transfer, personal care tasks, first aid and CPR, special conditions, home management, home safety and sanitation, infection control, medically related activities and vital signs, and nutrition.

At least 20 of the 40 hours must be completed before the PCA has any client contact. The remaining 20 hours must be completed within six months of the date the PCA's training began. The Administrator tracks the six-month date on the training log and schedules the remaining hours so the deadline is not missed.
The directing RN or equivalent professional signs the training roster. The roster lists the date, hours, topics, trainer name and credentials, and any test results.

Before assigning any task to a PCA, the supervisor observes the PCA perform it or has the PCA demonstrate it. The supervisor documents a written competency determination for each task on the competency checklist. If competency is not shown, the PCA is retrained and re-evaluated before being assigned the task.

Before a PCA is assigned to a client with a special condition, the supervisor provides or arranges training specific to that condition. The PCA's competency is then demonstrated and documented. Without this, the PCA is not assigned to that client.

Before a companion/sitter works with clients, the supervisor confirms that the individual can read, write, follow instructions and complete reports. The supervisor also confirms training or demonstrated competency in: the needs of elderly, handicapped or convalescing persons; meal preparation; transport and escort; housekeeping and sanitation; home safety; handling medical emergencies; and infection control. This is documented.

The Administrator does not assign a companion/sitter to personal care or nursing tasks unless the individual is also qualified as a PCA or nurse and has a documented competency determination for the task.

Each employee who has completed one year of employment must complete at least 8 clock hours of in-service training in each year after that. Topics must relate to the employee's duties, such as infection control, client rights, dementia care, safe transfers, emergency response, abuse and neglect reporting, and documentation.
The Administrator builds an annual training calendar and reviews the training log monthly. Employees who are behind are scheduled for make-up sessions at least 60 days before their annual due date.

A qualified supervisor evaluates each employee in writing at least once a year by direct observation or demonstration of the tasks the employee performs. Results are discussed with the employee and signed by both (see PER-09).
Training and orientation time is paid time (see PER-06).
The Administrator files all orientation records, rosters, certificates, test results and competency evaluations in the employee's personnel record (see PER-05) and keeps trainer credentials on file.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures no employee works with clients before orientation; maintains the training calendar and log; keeps the six-month PCA deadline; ensures the training program is directed by an RN or equivalent professional.
Conducts or directs training, observes and documents competency, and evaluates employees at least annually.
Attends and completes required training, demonstrates tasks as asked, and reports training needs.
Does not assign any employee to a client or task unless the personnel record shows required training and competency.

documentation: Orientation checklist signed by employee and trainer
PCA training roster (dates, hours, topics, trainer credentials, test results)
Copies of nurse aide or other qualifying credentials
Written competency evaluations by task
Special-condition training and competency records
Annual in-service log showing at least 8 clock hours
Annual written evaluation

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees and contractors who provide client services or supervise services
policies.purpose: To protect clients and staff from the spread of tuberculosis and hepatitis by requiring TB screening at hire and annually, by requiring employees to report exposure, and by removing contagious employees from client contact.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires documentation of a satisfactory TB screening test for every employee at the time of employment and annually after that. The documentation is kept in the personnel record. Employees must report any known exposure to TB or hepatitis. No supervisor may knowingly permit an employee who has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis to serve clients until the employee has been determined not to be contagious. Employee medical information is kept confidential.

definitions.definition: A TB test (skin test or blood test, as approved by the health department or occupational-health provider) with a documented date and a negative or otherwise cleared result. A positive result must be followed by clinical evaluation and clearance.
Known contact with a person who has active TB or a hepatitis infection in a way that could transmit the infection.
A determination by a physician, other licensed health care professional or the health department that the employee cannot transmit the disease to others.

procedures: During the hiring process, the Administrator tells each candidate that a satisfactory TB screening test is required before employment and annually afterward.

Before a new employee's first client contact, the employee provides the result of a TB test. The result must show the test type, date administered, date read (if applicable), result and the name of the person or facility that performed it. The Administrator reviews the result and records a satisfactory finding.

The test method is determined by health department or occupational-health provider guidance. The agency accepts a skin test or blood test from a qualified provider. The date and result are recorded in the personnel record.

If the result is positive or unclear, the employee does not provide client services until a physician or other qualified health care professional documents that the employee is not contagious. The Administrator files that clearance.
The Administrator tracks each employee's annual TB due date on the personnel tracking log. Employees are reminded 45 days before the due date and again 14 days before.
An employee whose annual TB screening is not documented by the due date is removed from the client schedule until the documentation is on file.

During orientation (see PER-03), each employee is told that they must immediately report to their supervisor any known exposure to TB or hepatitis, and any symptoms such as a persistent cough, fever or night sweats lasting more than a few days, jaundice or unexplained illness.
When an employee reports exposure, a diagnosis or symptoms, the supervisor immediately takes the employee off client contact and documents the date and reason in a confidential note.

The Administrator refers the employee to a physician, occupational-health provider or the local health department for evaluation and does not return the employee to client contact until a written determination states the employee is not contagious.

The Administrator reassigns or covers the affected employee's visits so clients are not left without care (see SVC-06 and SVC-12). If clients may have been exposed, the Administrator consults the local health department and follows its direction on notification.

For occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials, the agency follows the exposure procedures and any hepatitis B vaccination offers required under the federal bloodborne pathogens standard, as described in SAF-07.
A supervisor must never knowingly schedule an employee who has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis until the non-contagious determination is documented.

The Administrator keeps TB screening documentation in the personnel record as the rule requires. Other medical records, such as physician notes and diagnoses, are kept in a separate, locked file and are shared only with those who need them to carry out this policy.
The Administrator reviews TB and exposure records during the annual quality review (see GOV-04) to confirm no lapses.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies TB screening before hire and annually, tracks due dates, removes noncompliant staff from the schedule and maintains confidentiality.
Does not knowingly permit exposed or diagnosed employees to serve clients; documents reports of exposure; arranges coverage.
Obtains TB screening on time, reports known exposure or symptoms promptly, and stays off client contact until cleared.

documentation: TB screening result at hire and each year (type, date, result, provider)
TB due-date tracking log
Clearance statements for any positive results or exposure
Confidential exposure report notes
Records of schedule changes when an employee is removed from client contact

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: Administrator, office staff and all employees and contractors who provide client services
policies.purpose: To keep a complete, accurate, secure and inspection-ready personnel record for every employee, as Georgia Rule 111-8-65 requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a separate written record for each employee. Each record contains the items the Georgia rule requires, plus the supporting documents this agency also keeps for compliance. Records are kept confidential, are accessible only to authorized personnel, and are available to DCH during an inspection. The agency keeps personnel records for at least five years after the employee leaves. Payroll records are kept for at least three years as required by federal wage and hour recordkeeping rules.

definitions.definition: The separate file kept for each employee that contains the items listed in this policy.
A single bond or fidelity coverage that covers employees with access to client funds. It may be documented once rather than for each employee.
Authority to handle a client's money or accounts without a per-transaction limit or independent control.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) opens a separate personnel record for each employee on or before the first day of employment.

Each record contains: (1) name, address, phone number and emergency contact information; (2) a five-year employment history, or the complete history if shorter; (3) records of qualifications; (4) documentation of satisfactory TB screening at hire and annually; (5) the date of employment; (6) a job description or statement of duties; (7) documentation of orientation and training; (8) at least an annual performance evaluation; and (9) bonding documentation if the employee has unlimited access to client funds.

The record also contains: the employee's signed statement regarding abuse, neglect and exploitation history; background check and registry results (see PER-02); proof of credentials or license; written competency evaluations; and the signed acknowledgement of agency policies.
At hire, the Administrator collects a five-year employment history on the employment application and notes any gaps. Reference checks are documented.

The Administrator verifies and copies credentials (for example, nurse aide registry listing, nursing license, completion certificate for the 40-hour program) and files the copies. The Administrator confirms nurse licenses are current in Georgia (see PER-01).
Employment eligibility (Form I-9) is completed within the federal deadlines, and the I-9 is stored in a separate I-9 file, not mixed with the evaluations or medical documents.

If an employee will have unlimited access to client funds, the Administrator ensures bonding is in place before access begins and files proof. If the agency carries a universal bond, a copy of the bond and the list of covered employees are filed once and referenced in each applicable record (see SVC-15).
The Administrator reviews each personnel record at hire, at each annual TB due date and at each annual evaluation using the personnel record checklist, and corrects any missing items within 14 days.

Records are stored in a locked cabinet or in a password-protected electronic system. Access is limited to the Administrator, supervisors who need the information, and payroll staff. Medical information beyond the required TB documentation is kept separately (see PER-04).
Records are made available to DCH surveyors on request during an inspection.

When an employee leaves, the Administrator records the separation date and reason, collects agency property, and retains the record for at least five years after separation. Payroll and time records are kept for at least three years.
Records past the retention period are destroyed by shredding or secure electronic deletion, and the destruction is logged with date and name of the person who destroyed them.

If a record is requested by the employee, the Administrator allows review of the file under supervision. Any other release requires the employee's written permission or a legal requirement, such as a subpoena (see REC-04).

responsibilities.duty: Creates and maintains all personnel records, audits them using the checklist, secures them, and produces them for DCH.
Submit evaluations, competency findings and training documentation to the Administrator on time.
Provide accurate information and keep contact, emergency and qualification information up to date.

documentation: Personnel record checklist for each employee
Employment history, qualifications and credential copies
TB documentation, orientation and training records, annual evaluations
Bonding documentation, where applicable
Background check results
Form I-9 (separate file)
Payroll and time records
Record destruction log

policies.title: Wage, Hour and Overtime Compliance
policies.applies_to: Administrator, payroll and scheduling staff, and all hourly employees
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] pays all employees correctly for all hours worked, including overtime, travel time and training time, and keeps accurate time records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] complies with the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). Georgia's state minimum wage statute is $5.15 per hour, so the federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour applies to most employers, and the agency pays at least that, and pays more where its wage scale or Medicaid program requirements call for it. As a third-party employer of home care workers, the agency does not claim the companionship exemption from overtime for its employees. Employees are paid 1.5 times their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek unless an exemption clearly applies. No employee may work off the clock. The agency pays for required training and for travel between clients during the workday.

definitions.definition: A fixed, recurring period of 168 hours (seven consecutive 24-hour periods) set by the agency as [WORKWEEK START DAY AND TIME].
The hourly rate actually paid, including most bonuses and differentials, used to calculate overtime.
All time an employee is required or permitted to work, including client visits, paid travel between clients, required training and orientation, and required meetings.
An agency or other employer, other than the client or the client's family, that employs a home care worker.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) sets and documents a fixed workweek and pay period and communicates them to every employee in writing at hire.
Each employee is paid at least the federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour for every hour worked. Pay rates are set in writing at hire and in any change.

Because the agency is a third-party employer, it does not apply the companionship exemption to its caregivers. Overtime is paid at 1.5 times the regular rate for all hours over 40 in a workweek, unless an exemption has been reviewed and documented as clearly applicable to a specific position.

The Administrator checks the current status of 29 CFR 552.109(a) and related home care rules with the U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division (or counsel) at least annually and before any change in pay practices, and records the result and date.

Travel between clients during the workday is paid working time. Travel from home to the first client and from the last client to home is treated according to 29 CFR Part 785 and is documented in the pay practice.
Orientation, the 20 pre-assignment hours of PCA training, the remaining PCA training hours, the 8 annual in-service hours and any required meetings are paid time (see PER-03).

Caregivers record time through the electronic visit verification (EVV) system or the agency timesheet. The payroll clerk reconciles EVV times to the schedule and to timesheets before each payroll, and corrects errors with the employee's knowledge. Where EVV and timesheet differ, the explanation is documented.

Employees must not work off the clock, start work early or stay late without approval, or perform work after hours without recording it. The supervisor tells employees this at orientation and discipline is not applied to employees who accurately report time worked.

The Scheduler plans schedules to avoid unplanned overtime. If an employee is forecast to exceed 40 hours, the Scheduler notifies the Administrator in advance. Overtime that is approved is paid, and overtime that was not approved is also paid, but the employee is counseled.
Payroll is reviewed each pay period by the Administrator for accuracy, including overtime calculation, deductions and that each employee is paid on the regular payday.
The agency gives each employee a pay statement showing hours, rate, overtime and deductions.
The agency keeps payroll and time records for at least three years, as federal recordkeeping requires, and in the personnel or payroll file (see PER-05).

The agency registers with the Georgia Department of Labor as an employer for unemployment insurance and files required reports and pays required contributions on time. The Administrator confirms workers' compensation coverage obligations with the agency's insurance broker and keeps proof of coverage.

An employee who believes they were not paid correctly reports it to the Administrator. The Administrator investigates within 7 days, corrects any error in the next payroll or sooner, and documents the resolution. No employee is retaliated against for raising a pay concern.

responsibilities.duty: Sets pay practices, reviews payroll, checks federal rule status at least annually, ensures DOL registration and insurance coverage.
Reconciles EVV and timesheet hours, calculates overtime, issues pay statements and maintains records.
Schedules to minimize unplanned overtime and flags employees approaching 40 hours.
Record all hours accurately and do not work off the clock.

documentation: Written pay rate and workweek notice at hire
EVV records and timesheets
Payroll registers and pay statements
Overtime approvals and exception notes
Annual record of the check on federal rule status
Georgia DOL registration and workers' compensation proof
Pay complaint log with resolutions

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers and supervisors
policies.purpose: To set clear expectations for how staff behave in client homes and in dealing with client information, so clients are treated with respect and kept safe from exploitation.
policies.policy: All staff of [AGENCY NAME] treat clients with dignity and respect, and respect the client's property and residence. Staff keep client information confidential and disclose it only as the agency's records policy and Georgia rules allow. Staff keep a professional relationship with clients at all times. Boundary violations lead to discipline up to and including termination. Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported under SAF-01.

definitions.definition: The limit that separates the caregiver's professional role from personal, financial or social involvement with a client or family.
Any conduct that crosses a professional boundary, whether or not the client agrees or initiates it.
Improper use of a client's money, property or resources for the benefit of someone else.

procedures: At orientation, the supervisor reviews this policy, the agency's written policies and the employee's duties with each new employee, and obtains a signed acknowledgement (see PER-03).
Employees treat clients with courtesy and respect, honor the client's preferences and rights to accept or refuse services, and follow the client's service plan.
Employees respect the client's property and residence. They do not remove, borrow, use or damage client property, and they report any damage immediately to the supervisor.

Employees do not discuss clients with anyone outside the agency, and do not share client information with other clients, friends or family. Within the agency, client information is shared only with staff who need it to perform their jobs. Disclosure outside the agency happens only as the agency's records policy allows (see REC-04 and CR-03).

Employees do not post any client's name, image, address or information on social media or messaging groups, and do not photograph or record clients unless the client gives written permission and the supervisor has approved it.

Employees do not accept gifts, tips, loans, money, bequests or transport from clients, and do not borrow from or lend money to clients. The employee reports any attempt by a client to give such items to the supervisor, who handles the matter under CR-04.
Employees do not enter into personal, romantic or sexual relationships with clients, and do not take on private duties for clients outside the agency's service plan.

Employees do not work while impaired by alcohol, illegal drugs or medication that affects safety. They do not bring family members, friends, children or pets to a client's home, and do not use client phones, computers, vehicles or supplies for personal use.
Employees do not accept client-directed tasks beyond the scope of the service plan. If asked, the employee politely declines and tells the supervisor (see SVC-01).

Employees tell the supervisor right away if a client or family member asks for something that feels inappropriate, if the employee has a prior relationship with a client, or if there is a conflict of interest.

Employees report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of any client to the supervisor and as required under SAF-01, whether the suspected person is a family member, another employee or anyone else.

The supervisor investigates reports of boundary violations promptly, usually within 2 business days, interviews those involved, and documents findings. The Administrator decides on any discipline, which may include retraining, suspension or termination, and reports to the appropriate authorities when required.
No employee is retaliated against for reporting a boundary concern in good faith.
Conduct findings and any discipline are recorded in the personnel record (see PER-05). Client-related incidents are also recorded under SAF-02 or REC-03.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy, decides on discipline, and makes required reports.
Teach and model boundaries, review reports, investigate violations and document findings.
Follow all conduct standards and report violations or concerns promptly.

documentation: Signed acknowledgement of conduct policy
Boundary or conduct reports and investigation notes
Disciplinary actions in the personnel record
Related incident records

policies.title: Administrator and Supervisor Qualifications and Designation
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Administrator, RN/LPN supervisors and other designated supervisors
policies.purpose: To make sure the person who runs the agency and each person who supervises caregivers is properly appointed, qualified and documented as the Georgia rule requires.
policies.policy: The governing body of [AGENCY NAME] appoints an Administrator who has full authority and responsibility for the agency's operations. In an owner-operated agency, the owner may serve as Administrator. The Administrator meets the qualifications of the rule. Every service is supervised by qualified staff. Supervisors must be qualified by education, training and experience, and the agency documents that determination in writing. A licensed RN or LPN supervises personal care for medically frail or compromised clients. If the agency offers nursing, a fully licensed Georgia RN supervises those services. Companion/sitter services may be supervised by an RN, an LPN, the Administrator or another staff member assigned the responsibility.

definitions.definition: The person appointed by the governing body with full authority and responsibility for the agency's operations.
A person designated in writing to oversee caregivers, complete service plans, make supervisory home visits and evaluate staff.
A client whose health condition requires nursing oversight of personal care (see SVC-13).
A satisfactory determination from the Georgia fingerprint-based criminal records check process described in PER-02.

procedures: The governing body appoints the Administrator in a signed, dated written resolution or appointment letter that states the Administrator has full authority and responsibility for operations. A copy is kept in the agency's governance file (see GOV-01).

Before the appointment takes effect, the governing body verifies and documents that the Administrator: (a) has no credible evidence of abuse, neglect, exploitation or deprivation of a client; (b) has completed any orientation and training DCH requires of administrators; (c) has made no material false statements to DCH or in applying for the position; and (d) has a satisfactory fingerprint records check determination. The agency applies item (d) as a requirement because the current text of the rule includes it.
The Administrator's file is kept as a personnel record (see PER-05) and includes a written job description, the verification documents and any required training certificates.

The governing body names a person to act in the Administrator's absence ([ALTERNATE ADMINISTRATOR NAME]). That person must meet the same qualifications. The name and phone number are posted in the office and given to staff.

Before assigning any person to supervise caregivers, the Administrator makes a written determination of the person's qualifications by education, training and experience in home care or nursing. The determination notes the supervisor's relevant education, licenses, work experience and training, and is signed and dated by the Administrator and filed in the supervisor's personnel record.

The agency uses an RN or LPN to supervise personal care for any client identified as medically frail or medically compromised. The supervisor verifies the nurse's license is current and in good standing and keeps a copy in the personnel record.
For medically frail or compromised clients, a registered nurse completes the initial service plan (see SVC-03 and SVC-13).

If the agency provides nursing services (SVC-14), it employs a fully licensed Georgia RN as supervisor. The Administrator verifies the license at hire and at each renewal date, and removes the RN from the supervisory role if the license lapses or is restricted.

For companion/sitter services, the Administrator designates in writing who completes the service plan and supervises: an RN, LPN, the Administrator or another assigned staff member. The designation is signed and filed.

Supervisors make supervisory home visits at the intervals required for the type of service and the level of care the client needs, following the schedule in SVC-04. The agency's practice is to use the shorter interval whenever there is any doubt about which applies, or when a complaint raises a serious question about services.
Supervisors evaluate each caregiver in writing at least annually by direct observation or demonstration (see PER-09).

The Administrator will not allow a supervisor to knowingly permit an employee who has been exposed to or diagnosed with TB or hepatitis to serve clients until the employee is determined not to be contagious (see PER-04).
Each Administrator and supervisor has a written job description that states duties, reporting line and authority. It is given to the person at appointment and kept in the personnel record.

The governing body reviews the Administrator's appointment and the list of designated supervisors at least annually and whenever a person leaves or a role changes. If the Administrator changes, the agency makes any required notice to DCH within the required time (see REC-02).
If a supervisor is found not to meet qualifications, the Administrator removes the person from the supervisory role immediately, reassigns supervision to a qualified person and documents the change.

responsibilities.duty: Appoints the Administrator, verifies qualifications, designates an alternate and reviews the appointment annually.
Determines and documents supervisor qualifications, verifies licenses, assigns supervisors in writing and maintains job descriptions.
Supervise services within their qualifications, complete service plans, make supervisory visits and evaluate staff.

documentation: Written appointment of Administrator
Verification of Administrator qualifications and fingerprint records check determination
Alternate Administrator designation
Written supervisor qualification determinations
Nursing license verifications
Written designation of companion/sitter supervisor
Job descriptions

policies.title: Annual Performance Evaluation and Competency Observation
policies.applies_to: All employees who provide or supervise services, including personal care aides, companion/sitter staff, nurses and supervisors, and the supervisors who perform evaluations.
policies.purpose: To make sure every employee who serves clients is competent in every task the job requires, and that this is checked in writing at least once a year by direct observation or demonstration, as Georgia Rule 111-8-65 requires of licensed private home care providers.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] evaluates each employee who provides services in writing at least annually. The evaluation is done by the employee's qualified supervisor through direct observation or demonstration of the tasks the employee performs. Competency is determined for ALL required job tasks, not a sample. Observations take place in the client's home whenever possible. Each evaluation records the tasks observed and the result. Any gap leads to retraining and a repeat evaluation before the employee is considered competent. The signed evaluation is kept in the employee's personnel record. An employee who has not been evaluated by the due date is not left unsupervised on the schedule until the evaluation is completed. Nursing personnel are evaluated by the agency's Georgia-licensed RN supervisor if nursing services are offered.

definitions.definition: A supervisor watches the employee perform the task with a client, or the employee demonstrates the task to the supervisor. A written test or a review of paperwork alone does not meet this standard.
The demonstrated ability to perform a required job task safely and correctly, according to the client's service plan and agency policy.
A written performance evaluation completed at least once in each 12-month period, counted from the date of hire or from the last evaluation.
